cia-0000112332: State Center for Study of Ufo's Established is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112332, dated March 1, 1990. The title reports a new state center for the study of UFOs. Established is the heading's word for its founding, in the title itself. The brief record shares its date with a companion UFO item on sightings near Moscow.
cia-0000112832: Juan Tria - Espionage is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112832, dated October 1, 1945. The title pairs a name and a charge in three words: Juan Tria, espionage. No place or act is stated in the heading itself. The brief record is a name and charge file from the autumn of 1945 in the wartime files.
cia-0000119732: Filed in the Eastern Europe series in September 1956, this CIA report covers the situation in Hungary. The regional roundup placed Budapest's growing crisis inside the wider unrest of the Soviet bloc that autumn. Regional framing mattered because trouble in one satellite state tended to echo in the others, a pattern the series was built to catch early.
cia-0000120632: An August 1962 CIA memorandum records a meeting with the President about Cuba. It was written two months before the missile crisis brought the two superpowers to the brink. Kennedy's White House was already deep in Cuba planning, and the paper preserves what was said while the stakes were still hidden.
cia-0000124332: A January 1960 CIA document holds information on American prisoners of war who had not been repatriated, the word information misspelled in the heading. Years after the Korean fighting ended, some Americans had still not come home. The paper preserves what the agency knew of their cases. Non-repatriates were the hardest cases of the war's aftermath, men whose fate turned on politics in Beijing rather than on any list the armistice had produced.
cia-0000126932: Filed around January 1983, this untitled CIA document is a list of names and memberships. No title or purpose was recorded with it in the file. Rosters of this kind were raw material for counterintelligence work, and the paper preserves the list as it was filed. Bare rosters frustrate readers by design of their filing, yet names and memberships together form the raw graph from which network studies of groups are built.
cia-0000132232: Situation report 549, from January 1991, gives the status of the oil spill along with political developments, the heading breaking off. The spill was spreading along the Gulf coast as a deliberate act of war. The report tracks both the slick and the politics around it. Pairing the spill with politics in one heading captures the crisis exactly: the oil was at once an environmental disaster and a lever in the bargaining.
cia-0000132432: Cuban arms purchases fill a CIA document dated January 2, 1960. The new revolutionary government was shopping for weapons in several markets. Washington watched each shipment and each rumor of one with close care. Arms deals would soon become the hard currency of Cuba's new Soviet ties. The short document tracks the purchases known to analysts at the start of that year.
cia-0000132632: Events in Cuba are surveyed in a CIA paper dated June 1, 1960. By the middle of that year the word developments had come to mean seizures of firms, deals with Moscow, and a break with Washington drawing near. The file was growing too fast for colorful titles by then. The short paper gathers the latest events as analysts recorded them.
cia-0000135832:
A Study of Assassination is a short CIA training text tied to the Guatemala operation, with an estimated date of January 1954. It was written for PBSUCCESS, the covert plan against President Jacobo Arbenz, and the record lists the agency itself, not a single author, as its creator. Few papers in the whole file carry a plainer title, or a darker one.

Inside, the study treats killing a chosen leader as planned work, weighing how a target should be picked and how the act should be done and hidden. Long kept secret, the paper later became the best known and most condemned text of the Guatemala operation. Readers still cite it when they ask how far the agency was willing to go in 1954.
cia-0000135932: A cable of 1 January 1954 survives in the declassified CIA files, dealing with follow-up on the public reply to a white paper. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136232: The record dated 3 May 1954 is a declassified CIA situation report about daily operations situation report number 3, the countdown series running in May 1954. Guatemala in these years meant PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against President Jacobo Arbenz and the government he led. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136932: Loads of arms are landing at Toncontin field, a source in Tegucigalpa reports in April 1954. He says it is common knowledge there. Planes land and stay only minutes. They unload fast, then take off again. A second source doubts the tale. It fits nothing he knows, he says. He asks how the first man reached his findings. Did anyone read insignia through overpainting? No. The report went to Playdon at once on receipt.
cia-0000137332: Communist bloc approaches to Cuba continue, this NSC briefing states. It is dated 24 July 1960. A memorandum for the record transmits the paper. A trade pact was concluded with Communist China on 23 July. It marks a strong Chinese effort at recognition from Cuba. It also shows Peking's willingness to back an anti-American move. Considerable material support stands behind it. The memorandum is a routing vehicle. It carried the briefing into the file a year before the Bay of Pigs.
un-ga-res-32:
Early in 1946 the UN General Assembly took up the case of Spain, then ruled by General Franco. Resolution 32 recalls two wartime pledges. At San Francisco, states set up with Axis help were barred. At Potsdam, the big three powers vowed not to back Spain's entry to the UN. The Assembly backs both pledges in full.

Members are urged to act in the letter and spirit of those pledges in all future dealings with Spain. The text stops short of a break in ties. But it marks Franco's Spain as a state born of fascist aid. As such, it is unfit for a UN seat while his regime lasts.
un-ga-res-a-69-32:
An arms race in outer space must be stopped before it starts, says Resolution A/69/32, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the shared gain of all mankind in the study and use of space for peaceful ends. It voices grave concern at the chance of weapons spreading to orbit, and recalls the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bars mass-kill arms from space.

The rules now in force, the Assembly holds, do not by themselves bar a space arms race. The legal frame must be made stronger and more firm. A draft treaty on the point, laid before the Conference on Disarmament, is welcomed as a step in that work.
un-sc-res-32: Fighting on the island of Java drew the Security Council back in Resolution 32, passed on 26 August 1947. Armed work by Dutch forces on the soil of the Republic of Indonesia still ran on. The vote calls both the Netherlands and the Republic back to the Council's call of 1 August 1947. That call had ordered a cease-fire and a peaceful fix to their fight. Both sides are told to hew to it in strict form.
un-sc-res-232: Dated 1960 in the catalog, Resolution 232 records formal action by the United Nations Security Council. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1332: Readers meet Resolution 1332 here as a Security Council record, catalogued with a date of 2000. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1532:
Former Liberian president Charles Taylor is the target of Resolution 1532, passed in March 2004. Taylor had gone into exile in Nigeria after Liberia's civil war, but the Council feared his money and allies could restart the fighting. The members voted to freeze his assets.

The freeze reaches Taylor, his family, and close associates, and it covers funds held in other countries. States must stop those people from moving or spending the money, with narrow limits for basic needs. The text is a clear case of the Council using money as a tool to guard a peace deal.
un-sc-res-1632: From 2005, Resolution 1632 records a decision of the fifteen-member Security Council in official wording. The source is English Wikisource's transcription of the UN record. Inside, the members first align on the facts as they state them, then vote the response. The untouched text is the primary evidence of that response, and it is kept whole.
un-sc-res-1732: From 2006, Resolution 1732 records a formal decision of the Security Council, preserved in official-record form. The transcription here is English Wikisource's. Inside, the members build their case in the preamble before acting in the operative part, a rhythm as regular as a court's. The whole performance is kept, so the reasoning survives with the result.
un-sc-res-1932: Kept under number 1932, a Security Council resolution survives in official-record form through English Wikisource. The act's preamble and operative paragraphs divide the labor of governing between them: one explains, the other obliges. The entry preserves the division intact, giving readers the complete instrument rather than an account of its effects.
cia-0000135732: This Spanish-language document from the 2506 Brigade files carries an estimated date of 1 January 1961. The brigade of anti-Castro exiles was in CIA-run training that winter. The catalog title flags the estimated date and gives no subject. Like its companions in this series, the item is preserved in Spanish as a primary source. Its description here rests on the record: brigade, language, estimated date, and declassified release.
cia-0000136632: Dated 3 February 1961, a Spanish text from the declassified files of Brigade 2506, the CIA-trained Cuban exile force. The brigade was about ten weeks from its landing at the Bay of Pigs. The catalog gives this document no subject heading. Preserved in Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, it is a dated piece of the brigade's paperwork from its final training stretch.
plos-pone-0000032:
Marina Bacac, Paolo Provero, Nathalie Mayran, and co-authors found a survival signal hiding around tumors in a 2006 study. The stroma is the supporting tissue that surrounds a tumor, and it responds when cancer invades. The team measured that stromal response in mice as tumors spread into it.

A gene pattern in the responding stroma predicted how long prostate and breast cancer patients survived. In other words, tissue that is not itself cancer still carries a forecast of the patient's fate. Doctors usually grade the tumor alone; this work argues the neighborhood matters too. Such signatures could one day help decide which patients need aggressive treatment and which can safely be spared it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d32: Alexander Kirk, the American ambassador in Egypt, wrote to the Secretary of State on September 10, 1943, and his dispatch is Document 32 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Kirk's post in Cairo put him at the hub of Middle East reporting, and his cables home fed Washington's picture of the region. Two months later his city would host the Cairo Conference itself. The record names no topic for this dispatch.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d132: Stephen Early wrote again on November 16, 1943 to Hull, Stimson, Knox, and the Secret Service chief, in a letter that is Document 132 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. It repeats the address list of his note of the day before, a sign of standing summit business passing through his office. The record gives the names and the date. The letter's business is stated in the printed Foreign Relations text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d232:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 390/1 aboard the Iowa on 18 November 1943, on future operations in the Southeast Asia Command. It answers a paper from the British side and guards the Combined Chiefs of Staff's right to decide more than grand strategy alone.

The American chiefs hold that the combined body should choose among courses of action, and fix their order and timing, for Southeast Asia. Since the United States cannot supply what Operation First Culverin would need, they agree that Operation Buccaneer should be mounted as early as possible. They also ask the Southeast Asia commander to study further land, sea, and air moves to pin down Japanese forces in south Burma.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d332: President Roosevelt sent Ambassador Alexander Kirk a one-line memorandum at Cairo on 26 November 1943. It asks Kirk to have Wadsworth, the American consul general at Beirut, come down to Cairo when Roosevelt returns there, which he expects to be about Thursday or Friday. The editors date those days to 2 or 3 December, during the second Cairo stay after Tehran. The brief note is signed only with the President's initials.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d432: Harry Hopkins sent Ambassador Steinhardt an urgent telegram from Cairo on 3 December 1943 about the greeting party for President Inönü of Turkey. Major John Boettiger is accompanying the President's plane to Adana that day, to extend Roosevelt's greetings to Inönü on his arrival and to travel back with him. Randolph Churchill is flying on a similar mission in the Prime Minister's plane. Hopkins adds a small point of ceremony and tactics in one line: the President would be pleased to have Inönü ride in the American plane.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d532:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt in Ankara wrote on December 24, 1943 to Paul H. Alling, chief of the State Department's Division of Near Eastern Affairs. Writing to a division chief meant writing to the desk that ran Turkish policy day by day. The State Department printed the letter in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Steinhardt's channel to Alling was where embassy reporting met Washington policymaking on Turkey and the Near East. Three weeks after the Cairo meeting with President İnönü, the Turkish question remained open and delicate. For readers, the letter shows diplomacy at the working level: an ambassador and a desk chief keeping a difficult account in order.
frus-1944-quebec-d32:
A second message from Harry Hopkins to Prime Minister Churchill is dated August 28, 1944. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume, next to its companions of the same date.

Hopkins divided his business among separate messages, a habit he shared with Churchill. His late-August letters to London prepared the Quebec meeting from the American side: who would come, what would be discussed, and what the President hoped to settle. For readers, this message is one panel of a day's concentrated staff work, valuable because it shows how much of a summit happens before the leaders arrive.
frus-1944-quebec-d132:
Myron Taylor, the president's personal representative at Vatican City, sent this urgent, strictly confidential telegram on September 1, 1944. It is addressed to Roosevelt and Hull, and it concerns Italy rather than the Vatican. Taylor wanted the president briefed by a man on the ground before the reported conference with Churchill.

Taylor urged a frank talk with General William O'Dwyer, who ran the economic section of the Allied Control Commission for Italy. O'Dwyer could explain Italy's relief needs and the plans to meet them, Taylor said. He asked that Hull or Leo Crowley telegraph O'Dwyer at once, ordering him to Washington for consultation without delay.
frus-1944-quebec-d232:
General Deane reported fast movement from Moscow on September 13, 1944. Marshall's Octagon 10 arrived just as air force headquarters signaled the Warsaw project was scheduled for that very day. Deane and the two ambassadors saw Molotov, who arranged approval from the Red Army General Staff. General Spaatz was informed, and the mission was rescheduled for September 14.

Deane doubted that representatives needed to come to Moscow at all. Planning details, he argued, were better worked out in London; all Moscow needed to supply was Soviet approval, which the two missions could seek. The editors' note adds that bad weather later postponed the relief mission to September 18.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d32: Harriman wrote again on 27 December 1944, his second report to Roosevelt in two days from Moscow. The cluster of reports shows the ambassador working hard to prepare the president before the American delegation left for the Mediterranean.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d132:
Preventing a third world war is the single aim of this Treasury paper of 19 January 1945. Titled “Long Range Program for Germany,” it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume among the papers prepared as the Big Three meeting neared. No author is named on the document itself.

Germany, it argues, must be rendered weak in politics, arms, and wealth, and kept weak for many years. Any program that builds Germany up as a bulwark against Russia and communism will lead, in time, to a third world war. The paper admits no plan can promise peace. Its standard is therefore the opposite of a minimum program: see how far we can go now to make another German war impossible.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d232:
A Foreign Office man's fears about Iran fill this cable of 2 November 1944 from London. Waldemar Gallman, counselor of the American embassy, reports the talk to the Secretary of State. The cable is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

The British government, the official said, is gravely concerned at the Russian attitude in the oil deadlock. If Iran gives in, the concession would be one large step toward folding northern Iran into the Russian orbit for good. The Soviet request, he added, was unlimited in scope. Unlike the British or Americans, the Russians never named the royalties they would pay. He went on to list other Soviet moves, from bought newspapers carrying Moscow's line to pressure inside the joint censorship committee in Iran.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d332:
Staying at Yalta instead of going back to Malta was the liveliest item before the Joint Chiefs on February 5, 1945. A British proposal suggested a change of plan. The Combined Chiefs would finish their open work at Yalta — called Magneto in the code names — and drop the return to Malta, called Cricket. Admiral Leahy put the idea open for debate.

General Marshall called the change agreeable, the next best thing to his own wish. He would rather have sent the American shipping men to Yalta instead. The minutes show war planning bent around planes, ships, and where tired staffs could sleep.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d432:

Eden interrupted with news: a strong cable from the War Cabinet rejected the earlier basis of discussion. Unless something like his text of three days before could be had, London would approve no formula.

Eden handed over a revised formula. A lively argument followed over whether it was a new text or just a change to the American one. Molotov objected to treating it as new. The minutes show allies bargaining past 10 p.m., with London's cabinet pulling one way and Moscow the other.

frus-1945-potsdam-1-d132:

The memo to his British counterpart is document 132 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It gives the party's route and arrival time so the British could track the flight.

Two aircraft, a C-54 and a C-47, will carry them on to Babelsberg, though their numbers are not yet known. frus-1945-potsdam-1-d232:

frus-1945-potsdam-1-d332:
Army planners on the Joint Strategic Survey Committee weighed dismemberment of Germany in an undated memorandum, and advised against it. Cutting Germany into several states, they wrote, would not fully break the aggressive nationalism of the past century. New small states in central Europe would instead widen the field for rivalry among the great powers.

From a long-range military and political view, the committee called substantial dismemberment undesirable. It raised no objection, though, to fair border changes sought by Denmark, the Netherlands, and Belgium. The extract reached President Truman through Admiral Leahy, though the Joint Chiefs had not approved the committee's views as their own.

frus-1945-potsdam-1-d532:

frus-1945-potsdam-1-d632:

arxiv-2606-04932: In hot, electrically charged gas called plasma, magnetic Alfvén waves can break apart into other waves — a process called parametric decay instability. The simulations sharpen our picture of how energy moves through plasma.
arxiv-2606-05132: Planets are born in swirling disks of gas and dust, and formaldehyde drifting in those disks traces the chemistry of that nursery. The observations reveal how the ingredients of planets vary from star to star.
arxiv-2606-05532: AI assistance makes individuals more creative — but what does it do to the group? arxiv-2606-05632: Turning informal mathematics into Lean code — formalization — is painstaking human work that AI might accelerate. arxiv-2606-05732: The 1859 Carrington Event fried telegraphs; a repeat today could cripple satellites. arxiv-2606-07132: The quasi-biennial oscillation — stratospheric winds flipping every two years — may be tidally triggered. arxiv-2606-07232: Tau leptons' weak dipole moments probe heavy new physics — and constraints are tightening. This paper gives current and future constraints from those moments. François Rabelais told of the giants Gargantua and his son Pantagruel in a five-book comic epic, presented complete in the Urquhart and Motteux translation. The giants eat, drink, learn, travel, and philosophize through a France of monks, lawyers, and pedants. Every pomposity meets earthy laughter, often at enormous length and volume.

Beneath the bawdiness lies a humanist manifesto for education, tolerance, and appetite for life. Its most famous invention, the Abbey of Theleme, runs on a single rule: Do What Thou Wilt. Urquhart and Motteux, translating a century later, matched Rabelais's verbal excess with their own. The result is English literature's happiest monument to learned laughter.

Andrew Lang, a Scottish scholar and storyteller, opened Myth, Ritual and Religion in 1887 with a challenge. Rival scholars claimed all myths were coded tales of the sun. Lang answered that so-called savage myths keep the earliest thought of mankind, and must be read on their own terms.

Volume one lays out his method, comparing Greek tales with the stories of peoples in Australia, Africa, and America. He finds the same puzzles about death, dreams, and ghosts everywhere. The writing is lively and combative, full of learning worn lightly. Anthropology's first great debate over myth begins in these pages.
tob-4214-10732:
Studies in Pessimism collects Schopenhauer's darkest short pieces in Saunders's translation. On the suffering of the world, he argues that pain is positive and real, while pleasure is only the brief absence of pain. Human striving, on his view, swings between want and boredom.

Other essays weigh the vanity of existence, suicide, and the short span of life. The tone is bleak, yet many readers find the honesty oddly freeing: lower the claims, and life disappoints less. Schopenhauer's wit keeps the gloom from turning dull. For a pure dose of his outlook in a small compass, no other selection serves better.

Svatmarama, a yogi of the fifteenth century, compiled the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, the classic manual of hatha yoga. After Patanjali's Sutras, no yoga text has guided more practice. The Sanskrit work teaches the way of force: training the body to steady the breath and mind.

Chapters treat postures, breath control, locks and seals of the body, and the rising of kundalini, the coiled energy at the spine's base. Svatmarama promises health, calm, and at last absorption in the divine. Teachers still quote his lists of asanas. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.

Volume four of Mead's Echoes from the Gnosis presents the Hymn of Jesus, drawn from the apocryphal Acts of John. On the night before the Passion, Jesus leads his disciples in a round dance, singing a hymn full of riddling lines. Mead translates and comments on the strange, lovely text.

I would be saved, and I would save, the voice sings; I would be loosed, and I would loose. Early Christian esotericism seldom survives in so pure a form. Verified from the 1919 edition, the small volume lets readers watch a Gnostic-leaning community at prayer, with its Lord dancing at the center.
tob-10032:
Virgil, Rome's best-known poet, began his career with the Eclogues, ten short pastoral poems. Shepherds sing, compete in song, and talk of love, loss, and land taken from its owners. Mackail's translation is the version named for this entry.

Most poems stage a song contest or a talk between herdsmen in a green, idealized countryside. The fourth eclogue stands out: it foretells a child whose birth will bring a golden age, a passage Christians later read as a prophecy of Christ. These poems set the rules for pastoral poetry, and writers imitated them for well over a thousand years.
tob-13532:
Johann Weyer, a physician who had served at courts in Germany, published De Praestigiis Daemonum in 1563. Its title means On the Tricks of Demons. Weyer wrote against the witch trials then spreading through Europe, at real risk to himself.

He argues that so-called witchcraft is largely illusion, fraud, and sickness of mind, above all in old women charged with crimes they could not do. The true deceivers, he says, are demons who fool judges into burning the innocent. The book first broke the logic of the persecution in print and armed later critics of the trials.
regardie-tree-of-life-1932:
Israel Regardie set out the whole theory of magic in The Tree of Life, printed in 1932. His ladder is the Kabbalah's Tree, with its ten spheres and its paths between them. Regardie was Crowley's former secretary and a deep student of the Golden Dawn.

He shows how rite, symbol, and god-forms map onto the Tree, and how the student climbs it. The book is a system, calm and ordered, where Crowley's own could be wild. It laid the ground for Regardie's later Golden Dawn work. Many still call it the clearest statement of his magic thought.
fort-wild-talents-1932:
Fort's last book asks what strange powers sleep in man himself. Wild Talents, printed in 1932, takes up latent gifts, poltergeist girls, and crime worked by occult means. It closes the four-volume pile of data the learned would not touch.

He tells of folk who start fires by a look, of killers traced by dreams, and of talents that flare and die. His claim is that man has wild powers, bred down and feared out of him by church and school. The book is Fort's last word on the damned. It points his whole work at the reader's own skin.
morrell-narrative-four-voyages-1832:
Benjamin Morrell sailed on four long trade and seal trips in the 1820s. His Narrative of Four Voyages came out in 1832. The tales range wide, from the Pacific to the far south seas. One claim in the book still sparks debate to this day.

Morrell said he found a coast he called New South Greenland in the far south. Later sailors could not find that land where he placed it. Some call him a liar, while others think he erred in his charts. The book stays at the heart of talks on early Antarctic finds.
austin-province-jurisprudence-1832:
John Austin published The Province of Jurisprudence Determined in 1832. Austin, a former soldier turned law professor in London, set out to define what law is and where its study should stop. The book grew from his lectures at the new University of London.

Law, Austin argued, is the command of a sovereign, backed by the threat of punishment. That command theory cut law loose from morals: a rule can be law and still be wicked. Critics have fought the theory ever since, but it founded legal positivism, the school that studies law as it is, not as it ought to be. Austin's dry book shaped how the English-speaking world teaches law's first questions.
irving-alhambra-1832:
Washington Irving lived for a time inside the Alhambra, the old Moorish palace at Granada in Spain. Out of that stay came Tales of the Alhambra, published in 1832. The book mixes travel sketches of the palace and its city with legends told by local guides and servants.

Irving describes ruined courts, towers, and fountains, then retells the tales tied to them. Readers meet enchanted Moorish kings, hidden treasure, and lovers parted by fate. His warm, curious tone made Spain look romantic and storied to English readers. For many years it stayed the best-known American travel book about Europe.
berossus-chaldaean-fragments-cory-1832:
Berossus, a priest of Babylon, wrote the Babyloniaca in Greek around 280 BCE to tell the Greeks the true history of his own land. His three books are lost, but later writers quoted pieces of them. Isaac Preston Cory printed those fragments in 1832, and he added kindred scraps from Abydenus, Megasthenes, and Alexander Polyhistor.

The fragments give the Babylonian story in Babylonian terms: the making of the world, the great flood, and the long lists of kings from before it. They run on through Nebuchadnezzar and the fall of Babylon to Persia. Berossus stays our key native source for the king lists and dates of Mesopotamia.
manetho-fragments-cory-1832:
Manetho, an Egyptian priest, wrote the Aegyptiaca in Greek around 280 BCE to set out the true line of Egypt's kings. His book is lost, but church writers and chronologers quoted its lists. Isaac Preston Cory printed the fragments in 1832, with kindred Egyptian scraps from other hands.

The lists run from gods and demigods through thirty dynasties of human kings, the frame on which all dating of pharaonic Egypt still rests. Manetho gave the dynasties the names and order that scholars use today. These dry lines of kings are among the most used pages in Egypt's study. Cory's gathering keeps them in one place.
asclepius-latin-1532:
The Asclepius is the one full Hermetic book that the Latin West kept through the Middle Ages. It was ascribed to Hermes Trismegistus and said to be the work, in Latin, of Apuleius of Madaura. The edition here is the Basel printing of 1532. The dialogue itself dates from the second to fourth century.

Hermes teaches Asclepius about God, the world, and man, the being who stands between earth and heaven. The famous lament for Egypt foretells a day when the gods will leave and the temples stand empty. Augustine quoted that passage against the pagans. The talk of statues breathed alive by rites made the book a byword for bold Hermetic claims.
berkeley-alciphron-1732:
Alciphron: or, The Minute Philosopher, from 1732, is George Berkeley's defense of Christian belief in dialogue form. Seven dialogues stage a debate between Berkeley's speakers and the freethinkers of the age. His targets, named in the evidence of the work itself, include Collins, Mandeville, and Shaftesbury, the wits who made unbelief fashionable.

Berkeley answers them on their own ground, with wit, learning, and close reasoning about language and morals. The minute philosophers of his title are men who magnify small doubts into systems. Alciphron is the fullest statement of Berkeley the churchman and controversialist. It shows the philosopher of vision turned defender of faith, in his most polished prose.
wolff-psychologia-empirica-1732:
Christian Wolff, the great system builder of the German Enlightenment, published his Psychologia Empirica at Frankfurt in 1732. The Latin title adds that the science is handled by the scientific method, step by ordered step. The first edition is the text here, and no public-domain English translation of the work exists.

Wolff treats the soul as a field for exact study: its powers of knowing and desiring, measured and defined. His empirical psychology sorts what experience shows before reason builds its higher system upon it. The book's methodical order shaped how German universities taught the mind for a century. Kant grew up in Wolff's shadow and spent his career escaping and honoring it at once.
laplace-mecanique-celeste-bowditch-vol-2:
Bowditch's English Mecanique Celeste reached its second volume in 1832, again with his full commentary. Pierre-Simon Laplace devoted books three to five to the shapes and motions of heavenly bodies. Their topics include the figures that spinning planets take. Tides and the rotation of the Earth also receive full treatment.

Laplace works out how gravity shapes seas and worlds alike. Bowditch guides English readers through each hard passage step by step. The volume forms the middle of a four part translation. It shows French math astronomy at its peak strength. Students of the era learned the field from these pages. The commentary alone earned lasting praise.
roy-translation-veds-1832:
Rammohun Roy opened Hindu scripture to English readers in his Translation of Several Principal Books, Passages, and Texts of the Veds. The second edition of 1832 gathers his renderings of Upanishadic and Vedantic passages. Roy, a Bengali scholar writing in two worlds, argued that the oldest texts teach one God, not many idols.

His translations armed India's reformers and startled Britain's scholars at once. The book stands as a founding document of Hindu reform and of the Bengal Renaissance that followed. Roy's English versions were the first by an Indian hand, which gives them their landmark place.
shahnameh-atkinson-1832:
James Atkinson Englished Ferdowsi's Shahnameh in 1832, the first English translation of Persia's national epic. The Oriental Translation Fund issued his rendering, abridged in a mix of prose and verse. Kings and heroes of ancient Iran parade through its pages, from the first rulers to the fall of the Sassanian throne.

Rostam's feats, Sohrab's tragic duel, and the long grief of empires fill the Shah Nameh's vast span. Ferdowsi spent decades singing Persia's past back to itself after conquest. Atkinson's shortened version, for all its cuts, first let English readers feel the epic's scale and sorrow.
fielding-old-debauchees-1732:
The Old Debauchees, a farce of Fielding's early stage years, was first played in 1732. It is also known as The Miser Punished in some printings of his plays. Young Fielding was then the busiest comic playwright in London, turning out pieces at speed.

The plot turns on rakes, guardians, and young lovers outwitting age and greed, in the brisk manner of the Drury Lane farce. Songs, disguises, and sharp talk keep the short piece moving. Fielding's stage career ended when the Licensing Act of 1737 shut his theatre down, pushing him toward the novel. This farce preserves the sparkle of the playwright he first was.
plos-pone-0003432:
Mathieu Tilquin and co-authors followed a mosquito control microbe in nature in this 2008 study. Chemical sprays harm the environment and human health, so growers seek safer options. One option is Bti, a bacterium whose spores kill mosquito larvae. The team checked how long Bti lasts in real mosquito habitats.

Bti stayed present in those habitats for a long time after spraying. Long persistence can be good, since it keeps killing larvae. It also raises questions about effects on other small life. The study gives spray programs real field data on staying power.
plos-pone-0003532:
Christelle Tougard and co-authors traced how common voles spread across Europe in this 2008 paper. Ice age climate cycles repeatedly reshaped where species could live. Temperate animals survived in refuges, then spread out again. Europe's colonization stories had been sketched in general terms.

The team combined molecular evidence with the fossil record. Together they gave a finer picture of vole colonization routes. Genetic lines and dated bones checked each other's stories. The result shows how climate swings redrew the map of biodiversity. Voles breed fast and range widely, which makes them good trackers of past change.
plos-pone-0003632:
Marcos Seoane, Pablo Iglesias, Teresa Gonzalez, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It examines what happens when cells lose the retinoblastoma protein, a key brake on growth. The team focused on how that loss changes the cell's response to DNA damage.

Healthy cells often answer damage by entering senescence, a halted state that blocks tumors. With retinoblastoma lost, that damage response shifts in ways that favor tumor growth instead. The study shows how one lost safeguard can weaken the whole defense that keeps early lesions from becoming cancer.
plos-pone-0003732:
Christine L. Huffard, Roy L. Caldwell, Ned DeLoach, and colleagues published this marine study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Tracking wild animals over time often requires marking them, which can harm rare species. For the octopus Wunderpus photogenicus, the authors tested a gentler idea based on looks.

They found each octopus wears a body color pattern that is individually unique. Photographs alone can therefore tell one animal from another. This photo identification opens long-term studies of lifespan and movement in a shy species prized by divers and hard to follow.
plos-pone-0003832:
Valeria I. Petkova and H. Henrik Ehrsson published this psychology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Writers and artists have long imagined swapping bodies with another person. Science had not investigated the experience. It touches a basic question: why do we feel ownership of the body we inhabit?

The authors created a perceptual illusion of body swapping in volunteers. Participants felt they inhabited another person's body rather than their own. The experiment probes how the brain decides which body is mine, a process at the root of the sense of self.
plos-pone-0003932:
Benjamin L. Kidder, Jim Yang, and Stephen Palmer mapped where two gene switches bind in stem cells in 2008. Embryonic stem cells keep their flexible state through networks of such switches. Stat3 and c-Myc are both needed for mouse stem cells to self-renew. C-Myc also belongs to the set that can reprogram adult cells.

Their PLOS ONE article charts promoter sites that Stat3 and c-Myc occupy genome-wide. Promoters are the DNA stretches that start gene activity. Knowing shared targets shows how the two switches hold cells in the stem state. The map aids work on growing stem cells for research and therapy.
plos-pone-0004032:
Nitish Agrawal and Ruma Banerjee studied an enzyme linked to high homocysteine in 2008. Cystathionine beta-synthase, or CBS, starts the path that clears homocysteine. Mutations in CBS cause the most common severe inherited high homocysteine. The team used a yeast screen to find CBS partners.

Their PLOS ONE article identifies human Polycomb 2 protein as a SUMO ligase for CBS. Adding SUMO tags changes how other proteins behave. Substrate build-up had been shown to inhibit that tagging. Their finding ties protein tagging to sulfur amino acid handling. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004132:
Tomáš Kučera and colleagues published this study of blood vessel origins in PLOS ONE in 2009. Animals with two-sided bodies share a common ancestor that already had a blood system. Yet invertebrates have no endothelial cells, the lining cells that form vertebrate vessels, so early tubes must have formed without them.

The paper asks how those first vessel tubes opened a hollow space, called a lumen, inside. The authors argue that the hollow formed at the basal surfaces of cells, the sides facing away from the tube's centre. Their account offers a possible route by which the earliest blood vessels in animal history took shape.
plos-pone-0004232:
Melha Mellata, Jeffrey Touchman, and Roy Curtiss published this plasmid study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Avian pathogenic E. coli causes a complex of diseases in birds, and its close relatives sicken people. Large plasmids, rings of extra DNA, are often tied to the virulence of these bacteria, yet they remain poorly characterised.

The team present the full sequence of plasmid pAPEC-1 from strain chi7122, a reference avian pathogen. They compare it with related plasmids to see which genes it carries. The sequence gives researchers a parts list for the tools this bacterium uses to cause disease.
plos-pone-0004332:
Alison Morse and colleagues published this pine genome study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gymnosperms, the seed plant lineage that includes pines, carry some of the largest and most complex genomes known, yet the elements involved are poorly understood. Gymny is a previously undescribed family of retrotransposons, jumping genes, in Pinus that is related to Athila elements of flowering plants.

The team used Gymny and other repeats to trace the evolution of genome size and complexity in pines. Genomes grow, in large part, by the copying of such elements. Pines show that process written very large.
plos-pone-0004432:
Hydrogen made by bacteria is a possible clean fuel, and Zhanmin Fan, Ling Yuan, and Ranjini Chatterjee worked to boost output from the gut bacterium E. coli in PLOS ONE in 2009. Left to itself, E. coli makes some hydrogen when it grows without oxygen. It does so by breaking down a compound called formate, using an enzyme system built for that task.

The team reworked the bacterium's gene controls to push more of its sugar feed toward hydrogen. They changed the regulators that govern the relevant genes. The result, as the title states, was increased hydrogen production from glucose. Work like this matters because it tests whether cheap, farmed microbes can make fuel gas at a useful scale.
plos-pone-0004532:
Laser scans and three-dimensional models give better estimates of how much dinosaurs weighed, show Karl Bates, Phillip Manning, David Hodgetts, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Estimates of body mass are most reliable when a skeleton is complete enough to rebuild the body around it. Digital models are cheaper and faster than physical ones, and can be changed endlessly.

The team used laser imaging to capture skeletons, then built 3D computer models to estimate mass properties, including total mass and balance. How heavy a dinosaur was shapes everything else we infer: how it moved, how much it ate, how fast it could run. A transparent, adjustable method lets other researchers test the numbers instead of trusting a single artist's reconstruction.
plos-pone-0004632:
Squeezing a tumor slows its growth and can kill its cells, show Gang Cheng, Janet Tse, Rakesh Jain, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Compressive mechanical stress produced during growth in a confining matrix limits the size of tumor spheroids, balls of cancer cells grown in gel. Little was known about the dynamics of stress accumulation, how stress affects cancer cell phenotype, or the molecular pathways involved.

The team embedded single cancer cells in matrices and watched spheroids grow against resistance. Mechanical stress controlled spheroid size and morphology by suppressing proliferation and inducing apoptosis, cell death, as the title reports. Solid tumors are physical objects under pressure, not just genetic ones. This work helps explain growth patterns that pure genetics cannot.
plos-pone-0004732:
Chunjiang He and colleagues took a genome wide view of cancer specific message variants, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genes can be cut and joined in varied ways to make distinct proteins. That process shapes growth and disease, yet its role in human tumor growth was not well known.

The team built a search base and used a subtractive scan across the full set of messages. They sought variants found in tumors but not in normal tissue. A clean list of tumor only variants can yield new markers. It may also reveal weak points that drugs can target in cancer cells.
sismondi-italian-republics-1832:
J. C. L. de Sismondi wrote his History of the Italian Republics in 1832. The Swiss historian treats the medieval city-states of Italy in one sweep. Venice, Florence, Genoa, and Milan lead his tale of free towns.

Communes rise, fight, trade, and craft laws in his brisk narrative. Sismondi praises their liberty as a light in a dark age. Tyrants seize some cities while others guard their councils with pride. His book taught Europe to admire the communes of the Middle Ages. Readers meet banking, art, and war born in the same busy streets. The work remains a classic hymn to town freedom.
cia-0000009032:
How specialists compared prisoner-of-war photographs gets a full technical treatment in a March 1969 CIA paper. The authors lay out method for matching faces across poor images and long gaps in time. Their audience was other analysts doing the same work on live cases.

Good method protected the whole identification program from error. The paper likely covers features, measurements, and how to state confidence honestly. Readers today can watch a forensic routine being standardized in wartime. That routine later decided hundreds of individual case files. The document is thus a manual behind the search, not a report of one man.
cia-0000009532:
One American air force officer was killed and another captured in a single incident, a November 1972 report observes. The two fates, side by side, show how chance split crews who flew together. The report came during the war's final bombing season.

Paired outcomes forced officials to open two kinds of files at once: a death record and a prisoner case. Witnesses to the same event could serve both inquiries. The entry's plain wording carries that double weight without comment. It shows the accounting working at the level of one aircraft, one day, two very different men.
cia-0000009932:
Sightings of American prisoners moving through Laos lead an October 1971 item, followed by North Vietnamese and Pathet Lao regulations, cut off in the title. Transit sightings and written rules make an odd but useful pair. One shows the system in motion; the other shows it on paper.

Regulations told analysts what should happen to a captured man at each stage. Sightings showed what actually happened on the road. Comparing the two exposed the system's real workings. This file preserves both halves of that comparison, the moving prisoners and their captors' rulebook, in a single dated item.
cia-0000011832:
Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania were the three new states of East Africa, and a CIA paper from February 1967 surveys them together. Each had won freedom from British rule within the past few years. Their founding leaders, Kenyatta, Obote, and Nyerere, were setting very different courses for their young nations.

The paper compares the stability and direction of the three governments. It weighs their economies, their armies, and their leanings in the Cold War contest for Africa. Written with cautious optimism, the survey shows the independence generation in its first years, before coups and crises changed the region's path.
cia-0000013232:
Evacuation, escape attempts, illness, and detention fill a CIA paper from November 1970. Its subject is the human reality of the prison system. The paper follows American prisoners through the system's hardest passages. Men were marched between camps as fronts shifted around them. Some tried to escape into jungle that offered little mercy. Others sickened on short rations and endured cells built to break them slowly.

The paper catalogues that suffering in the file's calm hand. It may be the most human document in this whole accounting. For readers, it records what captivity cost, item by item, from the files of the side that waited.
cia-0000015332: A letter to Robert Palmer from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated March 3, 1961. Strong answers Palmer's inquiry of February 21, per the title. cia-0000015432: Money for the great official study of UFOs came through an Air Force contract with the University of Colorado, recorded January 2, 1967. cia-0000020332: A plot to assassinate President Castillo Armas, said to be planned by Captain Fernando Romero, fills a CIA record dated July 1, 1955. Plot reports of this kind were logged whether or not they proved true.
cia-0000022332: Soviet broadcasts of the Powers trial are kept in a CIA record dated in 1960. Radio carried the Moscow courtroom to Soviet homes and, through monitoring, to Washington. Broadcast text let analysts study exactly what the Soviet public was told. The trial was theater as well as law, and this entry holds the script as listeners heard it then.
cia-0000022532: Results of a photo comparison, case number blank in the released title, fill a CIA record dated in 1971. The missing number was cut or left empty before release. Photo comparison matched faces in enemy pictures against missing Americans, case by case. A result without its number is half a record, yet the finding itself was still worth keeping on file.
cia-0000028332: Honduras, its major towns and other important features, is surveyed in a CIA item dated in 1982. Town by town surveys were basic reference work, the gazetteer side of intelligence. Honduras in 1982 was becoming a base for the contra war against Nicaragua next door. A plain features list from that year quietly served a fast growing military interest.
cia-0000037532: An untitled CIA document dated September 2, 1971 mentions a source, whose name is deleted, who was shown photographs of missing men. The source's identity is blacked out in the released copy, so the file turns on what such a source could say about the photographs. Showing pictures to a source was a standard step in the MIA and POW work, since one recognition could settle a case. The redactions leave the method visible and the person hidden.
cia-0000045232:
Rivera y Damas warned that the kidnapping might hurt dialogue, in a CIA record dated August 1, 1985. Dialogue meant the slow talks aimed at ending the war itself. One crime, he feared, could poison a much larger peace.

Inside, the archbishop's caution about the talks is preserved. He had spent years building the bridges such talks would need. A kidnapping strained every one of those bridges at once. The file holds his warning from the case's opening days. It was spoken by the man who kept the idea of dialogue alive in that war.
cia-0000045932: A press release announced a joint United States and Vietnam search for missing American servicemen. A CIA item dated July 4, 1991, kept the text. Joint field work was a new step: former enemies digging side by side at crash and burial sites. The release marks the point where the accounting effort became open, shared work.
cia-0000049032: A CIA item from 1982 discusses whether Koos Koster matches a photograph of a man handing over money. Koster was a Dutch journalist killed in El Salvador that same year, which gave the comparison its charge. The item survives in the Truth Commission files, where photographs were evidence like any other record.

plos-pone-0004832:
Jon Oyer and colleagues showed that aberrant epigenetic silencing is triggered by transient reduction in gene output, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Aberrant silencing plays a major role in cancer by inactivating tumor suppressor genes. Endpoints are known, namely promoter DNA methylation and altered histone modifications, but triggers of silencing were not known. Leaving a gap in knowledge how stable repression first becomes established in a normal cell.

Brief output dips can lock genes off long term. That step explains how temporary events cause lasting change. Preventing the lock in may be possible. The finding reframes cancer epigenetics.
plos-pone-0005432:
Mihaela Balasu and colleagues mapped a meeting point between two proteins in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. One protein, ERK2, carries growth signals inside cells and is kept under tight control by partner proteins. No one had yet captured a clear picture of ERK2 joined with those partners.

The authors studied how ERK2 joins with PTP-SL, a major partner that holds its activity in check. They mapped the surface where the two proteins touch and how that contact works. Knowing that shared surface helps explain how growth signals are switched off and could guide new drug design.
plos-pone-0005532:
Masami Tanaka and co-authors reported a blood marker for acute leukaemia in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. MicroRNAs are short RNA strands that tune how genes are used. Their levels go wrong in many cancers, and some act like cancer drivers while others act as brakes.

The team found that one microRNA, miR-92, drops in the blood plasma of patients with acute leukaemia. A blood test for it could help doctors spot the disease and follow its course. Blood-based markers spare patients some painful bone marrow tests. A marker that falls and rises with the disease could also show early whether treatment is working.
plos-pone-0005632:
Amy Hurford warned about GPS errors in animal tracking data in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Collars and tags that record position by satellite are now standard tools for studying animal movement. Each recorded position carries some error, though.

Hurford showed that the error alone can create fake sharp turns in the path and strong false biases in direction. Models that ignore the error will describe the noise, not the animal. Her warning pushes ecologists to clean movement data before drawing conclusions about behaviour. The warning applies to birds, fish, and mammals alike, since all tracking studies share the same error source.
plos-pone-0005732:
Sunghee Choi and co-authors found in 2009 that common stomach-acid drugs also calm allergic responses. These drugs, proton pump inhibitors, block acid pumps in the stomach. A protein called TCTP, released by immune cells, helps drive allergy symptoms.

The team showed the acid drugs cut the release of TCTP from cells. Less TCTP outside cells means a weaker allergic signal. A drug already taken by millions might thus have a second use against allergy. The finding also hints that cell acid control and immune signaling are linked in ways worth mapping further.
plos-pone-0005832:
Stefania Trazzi and co-authors dissected in 2009 the tail end of a protein that helps build the centromere, the hub that pulls chromosomes apart. CENP-C is a core part of working centromeres in mammals. It carries distinct regions that bind DNA and partner proteins.

The team focused on its C-terminal domain and found it carries several critical jobs. Without them, centromeres fail to form properly and cell division goes wrong. Division errors are a root of miscarriage and cancer alike. Pinning jobs to one domain helps the field assemble the centromere's parts list in working order.
plos-pone-0006432:
Marie Billaud and colleagues examined how blood vessel walls talk to each other in PLOS ONE in 2009. The inner lining of a vessel, the endothelium, helps control how the smooth muscle around it tightens or relaxes. That control shapes blood flow in health and disease. Yet the two-way talk between lining cells and muscle cells was far from fully mapped.

The authors show that muscle cells also shape the lining's control of vessel response. Signals pass through tiny links between the two cell types. Reactive oxygen species, active oxygen-based molecules, carry part of the message. The result gives a fuller picture of how vessels tune themselves.
plos-pone-0006532:
Raymond Schuch and Vincent Fischetti explored the hidden life of the anthrax bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ecological and genetic factors governing anthrax reservoirs in the environment are obscure. A central tenet about the bacterium's life outside hosts rested on limited and often contradictory data. The authors reconsider how Bacillus anthracis persists in soil between outbreaks.

They highlight bacteriophage-mediated ecological adaptations: viruses of bacteria shaping the anthrax agent's survival. Phages can change what a bacterium does without changing its own genes permanently. This view may explain how anthrax lingers for decades in some places. It opens new questions for biodefense and ecology alike.
plos-pone-0006632:
Ahmed Hajri and co-authors put forward a fresh idea about how bacteria pick their hosts in PLOS ONE in 2009. Why a germ infects one host and not another is still poorly known for plant and animal pathogens. In plant germs, host range is often quite narrow. The team advance what they call a repertoire-for-repertoire idea. Type three effectors are proteins that bacteria inject into host cells to bend them.

They propose that the full sets of these effectors on each side are prime candidates for what sets host range. If the sets must match, that match could decide who gets infected. A clear, testable idea like this helps plan the next round of plant disease work.
plos-pone-0009432:
Rajesh Singh and co-authors wrote in PLOS ONE in 2010 about a surface protein of the germ that causes pneumonia. The protein is called PspA. Helper T cells, a type of immune cell, must spot parts of it for a vaccine to work well. The team mapped which small parts of PspA these cells can see.

They measured how strongly each part sticks to the immune markers that present it to T cells. Strong sticking matched a stronger T cell response. That link helps vaccine makers pick the parts most likely to train the immune system. It is a step toward a protein based shot against this lung infection.
plos-pone-0009532:
Theodore Sarafian and colleagues studied support cells of the brain in dishes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Astrocytes feed and guard nerve cells. A signal protein called STAT3 helps direct astrocyte behavior. The team blocked STAT3 signaling in astrocytes grown in the lab. They then checked the cells' mitochondria, which supply energy, and their levels of oxidative stress.

With STAT3 disrupted, mitochondria worked less well. Oxidative stress, a form of chemical wear, rose in the cells. So one signal switch helps keep the energy system of support cells sound. When support cells fail, nerve cells suffer too, which makes the link relevant to brain disease.
plos-pone-0009632:
Danika Bannasch and co-authors searched dog DNA for the roots of the flat face in PLOS ONE in 2010. Breeds such as pugs and bulldogs have short, broad skulls, a trait called brachycephaly. Because the trait is fixed within breeds, standard mapping inside one breed cannot find its genes. The team mapped across breeds instead, comparing flat faced and normal faced dogs. Shared stretches of DNA among flat faced breeds point to the cause.

The approach located genomic regions tied to the trait. Dogs' extreme variety makes them a strong model for skull genetics. Findings here may also inform human cranial disorders, since the same genes often shape faces in both species.
plos-pone-0010432:
Qiang Wang and co-workers studied a protein that helps blue-green bacteria handle low iron in PLOS ONE in 2010. These bacteria harvest sunlight with large antenna complexes. Iron shortage and other stresses reshape that machinery. Under stress, the team spotted two extra-large complexes beyond the normal trimer form. A protein called IsiA appeared in this picture. They tested whether IsiA is needed to build the large complexes.

Without IsiA, the super-sized complexes did not form properly. The protein also helped the cells switch energy flow efficiently between states. Such flexibility keeps photosynthesis working when conditions worsen. These bacteria shape oceans and once gave Earth its oxygen. Understanding their stress tricks matters for ecology and bioenergy alike.
plos-pone-0010532:
Deborah Kelly and colleagues published a study of the Notch receptor's outer structure in PLOS ONE in 2010; the article was later retracted. Notch passes fate decisions between neighboring cells during development. When Notch signaling fails in humans, diseases and birth defects follow. Knowing the receptor's shape should reveal how it works. The team used electron microscopy to picture its outer domain and how two copies pair.

Readers should note the retraction prominently attached to this record. A retracted paper remains in the scholarly record as a caution, not as reliable evidence. Its methods and claims failed later scrutiny. The entry is preserved so the history of the claim, and its withdrawal, stays visible. It should not be cited as sound support for Notch structure.
plos-pone-0010632:
Marjolein Meijerink and colleagues hunted the genes that let a probiotic bacterium steer immune cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lactobacillus plantarum is a friendly gut microbe used in fermented foods. Different strains calm or stir immune cells in very different ways.

The team compared strain genomes and matched the differences to immune responses. Dendritic cells, which teach the immune system what to attack, reacted differently to each strain. Certain gene regions lined up with stronger or weaker reactions. Knowing which genes drive the effect could help makers choose probiotic strains on purpose, not by trial and error.
plos-pone-0010732:
Anna de Breij and colleagues probed why one hospital germ succeeds so well, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Acinetobacter baumannii resists many drugs and has infected wounded soldiers and intensive care patients worldwide. Two candidate edges were biofilm growth, where germs coat surfaces, and direct dealings with human cells.

Clinical and non-clinical strains were compared on both traits. Biofilm strength and cell interaction varied by strain but did not cleanly explain which strains caused outbreaks. The germ's success likely rests on several traits at once, led by drug resistance itself. Infection control, the authors imply, must lean on hygiene and antibiotic care, not one trick.
plos-pone-0010832:
Anne-Sophie de Preux Charles, Valérie Verdier, Jennifer Zenker and co-authors published this diabetes study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Nerve damage is a common and painful effect of type 1 diabetes, yet the gene changes behind its start are poorly known. The team used Akita mice, which develop diabetes from a faulty insulin gene, to watch the earliest stage of nerve injury.

They tracked weight, blood sugar, and nerve signal speed during the first months of life to pin down when damage begins. Then they profiled gene activity in two nerve compartments, the dorsal root ganglia and the inner nerve tissue, before and just after symptoms appeared. Gene programs proved surprisingly steady as disease began. That resistance itself is a clue, suggesting early nerve damage may hinge on a few targeted changes rather than a broad gene shutdown.
plos-pone-0010932:
Jihong Li, Kazuaki Miyamoto, Sameera Sayeed and co-authors published this food poisoning study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The bacterium Clostridium perfringens makes an enterotoxin, CPE, that causes several gut diseases in people and possibly animals. The toxin gene sits in different DNA neighborhoods depending on the strain type, and the arrangement in types C and D was unknown.

Standard tests built for type A strains failed on type C and D isolates, an early sign their gene neighborhoods differ. The team cloned and sequenced the region around the toxin gene in selected isolates, then built a test to survey more. All seven type C isolates surveyed shared one arrangement. Li and colleagues map a toxin gene's address book, useful for tracing outbreak strains and judging which animals and foods carry risk.
plos-pone-0011032:
Anne-Laure Todeschini, Laure Teysset, Valérie Delmarre and co-authors published this fruit fly epigenetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. In flies, a jumping gene inserted near the chromosome ends can silence matching genes elsewhere in the genome, an effect passed through mothers and called trans-silencing. The team dissected which molecular machinery carries that inherited silencing signal.

Mutations in two genes of the piRNA pathway, the small-RNA system that polices jumping genes in the germline, strongly weakened the silencing. Silencing also tracked with accumulation of small RNAs from the target gene, and depended on HP1, a protein of tightly packed chromatin. Todeschini and colleagues connect a classic epigenetic puzzle to the piRNA pathway. Their work shows how mothers can hand offspring a ready-made defense, written in small RNAs rather than DNA.
plos-pone-0011132:
Marji, O'Donoghue, McClintock and colleagues studied a rapid aging illness in PLOS ONE in 2010. Children with this syndrome, called progeria, age far too fast due to a faulty form of a nuclear protein. The team traced how that fault disrupts a growth control signal in cells.

They found the faulty signaling could be reversed by blocking an enzyme that adds a fatty tag to proteins. That reversal points to a drug path already explored for this rare disease. Even a partial fix in cells brings hope for treatment. The work also informs research on normal aging, since the same protein is involved there.
plos-pone-0011232:
Barbosa proposed a network measure in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some puzzle like problems, such as coloring a map so neighbors differ, are far easier on certain networks than others. The author named that helpful quality conduciveness and tested it on coloring and independent set problems.

The measure aims to predict when a hard problem will yield to solvers quickly. That could save computing time by matching methods to networks in advance. It offers algorithm designers a new lens on why instances differ so much in difficulty. The idea links network shape to the phase changes known in optimization problems.
plos-pone-0011332:
Sonia del Rincón and colleagues set out in 2010 to build a better way to watch proteins being changed after they are made. Cells add small chemical tags to proteins, and those tags alter where a protein goes and what it does. Reading many tagging reactions at once, across the whole set of proteins, had been hard to do well.

The team built and tested a method that uses protein chips, with many proteins fixed in tiny spots on a slide. Samples run over the chip reveal which tagging activities are present and how strong they are. A reliable chip method lets researchers compare healthy and sick cells side by side. It can speed the search for tag patterns that mark disease or predict how a patient will respond to treatment.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1232:
Sato cabled Togo on 24 July 1945, after a short gap in the exchange. The Moscow bid was stalling in plain view. Soviet officials kept the envoy at arm's length while their own armies readied in the east, a fact hidden from Tokyo.

The report continues Sato's grim brief: soundings taken, doors still shut, hints that Tokyo's terms would not move Moscow. Two days later the Allies would issue their surrender terms from Potsdam. This cable lands just before that blow. It shows Japan's last channel to a softer peace closing, reported by the man who had to watch it close.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1332:
George Allen, deputy director of the office for Near Eastern and African affairs, wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on 25 July 1945. The note was sent while the Potsdam Conference was under way in July and August 1945. It was the last wartime summit of the American, British, and Soviet leaders. Allen's office handled American policy across the Middle East and Africa.

Readers get a staff-level paper from inside the department, written far from the summit table at Potsdam. Papers of this kind show how regional desks in Washington kept feeding views and facts to the men making choices in Germany. The note also shows the Near East holding a firm place on the wartime agenda even as the talks centered on Europe and Japan.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1432:
A fourth Soviet text dated 29 July 1945 continues the cluster of late submissions at Potsdam. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

By the fourth text, readers should be watching for the themes Moscow returned to again and again. Repetition in drafting is a signal of what a side values most. This paper adds weight to that signal. Set in the full run, it helps explain the shape of the final settlement. The points pressed hardest and latest were the ones the other leaders had to answer. In the protocol they granted, split, or refused them outright.
frus-1945-50-intel-d32:
Robert Lovett, assistant secretary of war for air, wrote to General Bissell, the Army's intelligence chief, on 23 October 1945. Lovett was one of the War Department's most able civilians. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Air power had its own intelligence needs, from target folders to reading enemy air strength, and Lovett watched them closely. His letter to Bissell shows the air arm stating its interest inside the Army's house. The name Lovett returns in the volume at the head of a committee on intelligence. Readers who note his early papers will see why he was chosen. Able men gravitated to this question in 1945, sensing it would shape the next war's opening days.
frus-1945-50-intel-d132:
Vandenberg wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 3 January 1947. The director of central intelligence opened the year with a letter to the board's senior secretary. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

January 1947 was the CIG's last season under the old charter: within months, Congress would debate the law that made the Central Intelligence Agency. Vandenberg's letter to Byrnes belongs to the director's campaign for that stronger future. Readers who have followed him since July can see the arc complete. He went from pressing the FBI over a hemisphere to pressing the cabinet for an agency. The volume ends its main run with the campaign still rising.
frus-1945-50-intel-d232: "Memorandum for the Record" bears the date 8 April 1948. It is document 232 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was in its first year, and the Council was taking up covert action for the first time. The form is a note to the file: no request and no order.
frus-1945-50-intel-d332:
Formal minutes cover a meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board, held on 20 November 1947. It survives in print as document 332 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The shift from the old group to the CIA was fresh. The Council was still learning how to run its side of the work.

A set of minutes does one job well. It fixes what a body took up and what it settled, in the order the items came up. Such pages are often the only proof of when a choice was made, and by whom. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d432:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 1, in the form issued on 19 January 1950, is document 432 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Directive No. 1 was the base rule of the whole series, so a new version mattered. Reissuing it in 1950 let the Council restate the CIA's core duties in light of hard use. Readers get the closest thing the system had to a founding charter, revised by experience. Later chiefs worked under versions of this first rule for the rest of the Cold War. Restating the base rule let each agency test its own habits against it once more.
frus-1861-d32:
Henry Sanford wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 30 July 1861, the same day Seward wrote to him. The dispatch is document 32 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Letters crossing in the mail were a fact of life in the age of steam. Neither man could know the other's latest word for weeks. The matched dates here let readers see two ends of one link, each writing in the dark about the other. Crossed letters fill this file, a sign of how far apart the two desks truly were.
frus-1861-d132:
Writing on 22 June 1861, William H. Seward addressed William Dayton, his envoy in Paris. The letter is document 132 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward wrote to Paris and to Brussels on the same June day. The twin letters show a chief working a whole front in one sitting. For Dayton, the note was fresh proof that France stood high in Washington's mind that summer. A whole front worked in one sitting shows the scale of Seward's daily labor. One sitting's work, spread across a map, shows a chief at full stretch.
frus-1861-d232:
Dated 2 April 1861, a report from Mr. Murphy went to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 232 in the President's message volume for 1861. It belongs to the month the Civil War began, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d32:
Seward's incoming mail for 13 March 1862 held a dispatch from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 32 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The letter comes from the winter of the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d132:
Seward's incoming mail for 22 August 1862 held a dispatch from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 132 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d232:
On 4 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Stuart, acting head of the British legation, in a letter printed as Document 232 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Lee's army was crossing the Potomac into Maryland as Seward wrote, carrying the war onto Union soil. European governments watched the invasion as a test of Southern strength. If the South won in Maryland, Britain might move toward backing it. Seward's letters in this window worked against that reading, and this one is part of the file that shows the effort. Both offices kept up the formal courtesies even when their governments were near quarreling.
frus-1862-d332:
On 8 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William L. Dayton a dispatch printed as Document 332 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister to France, posted in Paris.

Seward wrote while the French truce proposal waited on the British cabinet, the hinge of the fall. His guidance to Dayton in October mixed patience with plain warnings about what foreign action would mean. Letters like this one kept the Paris envoy aligned with the simultaneous effort in London, where the decision would be made. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d432:
Gabriel García Tassara wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 July 1862, a week after receiving Seward's last note. The letter is Document 432 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Resident ministers wrote often, and on small matters as well as great ones: a seized ship, a consul's complaint, a point of form. Each note from Tassara also told Seward, between the lines, how Madrid viewed the war that month. In July 1862 that view mattered, because Spain's ports in Cuba sat astride Confederate trade routes. The exchange preserved here is the working surface of a relationship both sides wanted kept calm.
frus-1862-d532:
A second reply of 7 June 1862 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Roest van Limburg at the Netherlands legation. It is Document 532 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's printed record.

Two questions, two letters: that was the Department's rule, and the Dutch file of that week obeys it strictly. Seward's paired replies matched Van Limburg's paired notes point for point. The business between the governments concerned Dutch trade and shipping. It concerned their rights and treatment in wartime. The Netherlands wanted no part of that war, except as a carrier. The exchange shows formal diplomacy at its most procedural, and its very dryness is what makes it a faithful picture of the work.
frus-1862-d632:
Edward Joy Morris reported from Constantinople to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 July 1862. The dispatch is Document 632 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Morris wrote as the Seven Days ended in Virginia, news that would take the summer to reach and be weighed in the Levant. His own subjects were the standing ones of the post: trade, protection, and the treatment of Americans under Ottoman rule. The independence of his file is its lesson. While the war consumed Washington, the republic's older foreign business went forward on its own momentum. It did so in places the war barely touched. Ministers like Morris were that momentum in person.
frus-1863p1-d32:
Three letters from London bear the date 16 January 1863; this one came from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Two more Adams letters in the volume share the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 32 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Three sheets in one day is a heavy day at any legation. Adams sorted his London news into parts: the cabinet, the press, and the Southern agents who worked the city. This dispatch is one of the three. It shows the scale of the post's work in a month when the war's meaning abroad was in flux.
frus-1863p1-d132:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 27 March 1863. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 132 in part one of the 1863 volume.

A three-letter day closed the legation's March mail in a rush. Adams had the cabinet, the press, and the shipyards to cover, and he gave each its sheet. This one opens the set of 27 March. The run of his spring letters is the record of a watch kept without pause, and this dispatch is a fair piece of it.
frus-1863p1-d232:
The Secretary of State, William H. Seward, wrote to his minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, on 11 July 1863.
