The letter is document 232 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d332: On 5 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 332 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d432:
28 March 1863 is the date on a letter from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d532:
On 25 May 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington wrote to Secretary William H. Seward. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d632:
From Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington: a letter dated 20 October 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020132:
Philipp Khaitovich, Gunter Weiss, Michael Lachmann, and their group proposed a neutral model of transcriptome change in PLOS Biology in 2004. The transcriptome is the full set of gene messages a tissue makes. The authors ask how much of its change over evolution is driven by selection, and how much is mere drift.

A neutral model gives the null case: change with no selection at all. Only data that beat that baseline need a stronger story. The team found much of the pattern fits drift well. That does not make selection rare, but it sets the bar for claiming it. The paper is a useful guard against over-reading gene data from any two species.
plos-pbio-0020332:
Shelly Beer, Anders Zetterberg, Rebecca A. Ihrie, and their team tested a cancer gene's timing in PLOS Biology in 2004. MYC is a powerful growth gene that can drive tumors when stuck on. The team switched it on in different tissues and at different stages of growth in mice.

The same gene took very different times to cause tumors depending on context. Some settings resisted for long spans, while others fell fast. That gap, called latency, shows cancer is not just about which gene breaks. The state of the cell counts as much. Results like this help explain why one mutation can be deadly in one organ and quiet in another.
plos-pbio-0020432:
Christiane E. Wobus, Stephanie M. Karst, Larissa B. Thackray, and their team grew norovirus in the lab in PLOS Biology in 2004. Noroviruses cause most cases of viral stomach flu, yet they long refused to grow in cell culture, which stalled research. The team's mouse norovirus system broke that barrier.

Grown in culture, the virus favored immune cells: dendritic cells and macrophages. That tropism, its taste for certain cells, shapes how infection starts in the gut. A working culture system lets labs test antivirals and study the virus life cycle at last. The mouse virus now serves as the stand-in for its human kin, which still resist culture.
plos-pone-0000132:
Ximena J. Nelson and Robert R. Jackson published this ecology study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It features a predator from East Africa that, as the title says, chooses malaria vectors as its preferred prey. Malaria vectors are the mosquitoes that carry the malaria parasite to people.

A predator that hunts those mosquitoes by choice is a natural ally in malaria control. The authors document this preference and what it means for the food web around it. The work drew attention because most predators eat mosquitoes only by chance; a specialist hunter raises the prospect of biological control of a deadly disease.
plos-pone-0000232:
Nooshin Tabatabaei-Zavareh, Anastasia Vlasova, Chelsea Pamela Greenwood, and colleagues published this stem cell paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Natural killer cells are frontline immune defenders, and making them in the lab from embryonic stem cells could supply therapies. The authors characterize the developmental pathway those cells follow as they grow from stem cells in vitro.

Knowing each step of natural killer cell development lets researchers steer and check the process. The paper maps that path in the dish. It supports efforts to grow immune cells on demand, a goal for cancer therapy where a patient's own cells are in short supply.
plos-pone-0000332:
Erik Cobo, Albert Selva-O'Callagham, Josep-Maria Ribera, and colleagues published this randomized trial in PLOS ONE in 2007. It asks whether statistical reviewers improve reporting in biomedical articles. Manuscripts were randomly assigned review with or without a statistician's input, and the quality of reporting was compared.

Poor statistical reporting wastes research and misleads doctors. The trial gives rare experimental evidence on an editorial practice usually adopted on faith. Its result speaks to journal editors deciding whether statistical review is worth its cost and delay. Good reporting is not a small thing: doctors act on what papers say. Weak numbers can mislead care, so proof of what helps is worth having.
plos-pone-0000432:
Jonas Dahlberg and colleagues linked a common gene variant to salt handling in the body, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The gene is NEDD4L, which helps control sodium channels in the kidney. The team tested whether a polymorphism in it goes with increased salt sensitivity. They also checked two hormone-related markers, P-renin and Nt-proANP, which moved in opposite directions.

Salt sensitivity, where blood pressure rises sharply with dietary salt, varies from person to person and runs in families. A gene that explains part of that spread could help identify who most needs to cut salt. The study connects a kidney sodium channel regulator to everyday cardiovascular risk.
plos-pone-0000532:
Andrés Muñoz-Alarcón and colleagues compared fly and human versions of a disease of the cell's scaffolding, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Lamins are proteins that line the nucleus and give it structure. Human mutations in them cause laminopathies. That family of disorders affects muscle, fat, and aging. The team characterized lamin mutation phenotypes in Drosophila and compared them to the human diseases.

A fly that shows the same cellular defects as a human patient becomes a fast, cheap model for testing treatments. Comparing phenotypes across species also shows which parts of lamin function are ancient. The study validates the fly as a stand-in for a group of rare but revealing human disorders.
plos-pone-0000632:
Hassan Khan, Ather M. Taqui, Muhammad Rizwanulhaq Khawaja and colleagues compared two ways of teaching medical students, in PLOS ONE in 2007. One group learned by problem-based learning, working through cases. The other followed a conventional lecture-based curriculum. The subject under test was health research: what students knew about it and how they felt about doing it.

The authors argue that medical curricula in developing countries should stress research training. Students who can judge and do research strengthen a whole health system. By comparing knowledge and attitudes side by side, the study gives curriculum planners direct evidence about which approach builds research-minded doctors.
plos-pone-0000732:
Wei Hou, John Stephen F. Yap, Song Wu and colleagues tackled the fine-mapping of trait genes in breeding experiments, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Mapping quantitative trait loci, or QTL, aims ultimately at cloning the actual genes behind farm and medical traits. Yet only a small portion, at most about one percent of detected QTL, had been characterized at the molecular level.

Their method haplotypes a quantitative trait using a high-density map in experimental crosses. Haplotyping reads the pattern of inherited blocks, not single markers. Denser, smarter mapping could raise that one-percent success rate. Breeders and medical geneticists share the same bottleneck, so a better method serves both fields.
plos-pone-0000832:
Harald Staiger, Fausto Machicao, Norbert Stefan and co-authors tied new diabetes risk genes to how well the pancreas makes insulin. Type 2 diabetes sets in when the body resists insulin and the beta cells that make it wear out. Diet, low activity, and a web of inherited traits all play a part. Genome scans had just found new risk spots, but not what they do.

The team's title states the link: variants in those new risk spots set beta-cell function. In other words, the risk acts through the insulin-making cells themselves, not just through insulin resistance. Knowing where each risk gene does its harm tells drug makers where to aim. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2007.
plos-pone-0000932:
Raquel Ferreira, Claudio Lazzari, Marcelo Lorenzo and colleagues asked how blood sucking bugs find veins under the skin, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Some of these insects slide their mouthparts straight into a vessel and feed from inside it. How they locate the vessel was largely unknown, and less than five percent of skin holds vessels at all.

The team tested whether the bugs read skin surface temperature as a guide. Warm patches could betray the blood flowing below. Knowing how a blood feeder aims matters beyond curiosity. These bugs spread serious diseases, and each step in feeding is a possible place to block them.
plos-pone-0001032:
Jae Hyang Lim, Hirofumi Jono, Tomoaki Koga and colleagues studied a protein that brakes inflammation from a common airway germ, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae causes respiratory infections in adults and children. The inflammation it triggers runs largely through NF-kappaB, a master switch for immune genes.

The tumor suppressor CYLD acts as a negative regulator of that switch. The team examined its role in middle ear and lung inflammation in mice infected with the germ. A natural brake, understood well, suggests how harmful inflammation might be eased without silencing defense. Ear infections in children are a major target.
plos-pone-0001132:
White blood cells must crawl out of the bloodstream and into tissue to fight infection. Jürgen Schymeinsky and co-authors traced one step of that journey in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They focused on Syk, a signaling protein found mainly in blood cells, and on a second protein, PI3K-delta.

The authors show that Syk controls the movement of PI3K-delta to the leading edge of a migrating white blood cell. That placement helps the cell build a lamellipodium, the flat front extension it uses to move. The pathway they map connects the cell's grip on blood vessel walls to its crawling machinery.
plos-pone-0001232:
Glycans, the sugar chains decorating proteins, are built step by step by many enzymes, and finding which gene makes which enzyme is slow work. Harumi Yamamoto and colleagues present a screening method in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They call it CIRES, for correlation index-based responsible-enzyme gene screening, and it uses DNA microarray data.

The logic is that an enzyme gene's activity should track the appearance of the glycan it builds. By correlating expression patterns, the method nominates candidate genes for a given step in glycan biosynthesis. Faster gene hunting matters for understanding diseases of abnormal glycosylation.
plos-pone-0001332:
Common painkillers, the NSAIDs, work mainly by blocking cyclooxygenase enzymes, but they have other targets too. Asher Peretz and colleagues explored one such target in new diphenylamine compounds, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Two NSAIDs, diclofenac and meclofenamate, had recently been shown to also affect potassium channels called M-channels.

The authors describe derivatives in which the function switches: cyclooxygenase inhibition fades and M-channel modulation takes over. M-channels calm neuronal excitability, so such compounds interest researchers in pain and epilepsy. The study is medicinal chemistry: reshaping a known drug scaffold toward a new target.
plos-pone-0001532:
Robyn Kim, Aaron Seitz, and Ladan Shams wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on learning with more than one sense. Most learning studies use sight or sound alone. Yet the senses work as a team in daily life, even at early steps. The team tested whether matched sight and sound cues help visual learning more than mixed ones.

Matched cues did boost how well people learned the visual task. The gain shows the senses aid each other when their signals agree. Training that pairs senses with care could speed skill gains. The result also shapes models of how the brain merges sense data.
plos-pone-0001632:
Martine Muleris, Alexandra Chalastanis, Nicolas Meyer, and their co-authors studied unstable chromosomes in bowel cancer for a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. In many tumors, cells gain or lose whole chromosomes or swap pieces of them, a fault called chromosomal instability. It can arise when normal chromosomes are sorted wrongly at cell division, or when chromosome structure is rearranged.

The team focused on tumors that stay near the normal chromosome number, called near-diploid colorectal cancers. They asked which chromosomes each kind of fault tends to hit. The full text gives the chromosome counts and structural changes they found, and the link they report between number changes and structure changes. Knowing which faults come first may help explain how these cancers grow and change.
plos-pone-0001732:
Thilan Wickramarachchi, Yengkhom S. Devi, Asif Mohmmed, and their co-authors identified a new malaria parasite protein in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Plasmodium falciparum causes the deadliest malaria. Its merozoite stage invades red blood cells, and proteins on the merozoite surface or released from its apical organelles are leading vaccine candidates.

The team characterized a novel merozoite apical protein, PfAARP, rich in the amino acid asparagine, and tied it to red cell binding and invasion. The full text gives the gene, the protein's location, and the binding tests. Each new invasion protein is a possible vaccine piece, since blocking invasion stops the parasite's blood stage, the phase that makes people sick.
plos-pone-0001832:
Elisabeth Fonteneau and Heather K. J. van der Lely measured brain responses in language-impaired children in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Specific language impairment, or SLI, affects over 7 percent of children. It is studied as a window onto the biological foundations of language and its evolutionary origins.

Recording electrical brain responses to language stimuli, the team found grammar-specific deficits in the children with SLI. The full text gives the response patterns for grammar versus other language features. A deficit confined to grammar supports the idea that grammar rests on its own brain machinery. That machinery is separate from general intelligence or vocabulary, which shapes how these children should be taught.
plos-pone-0001932:
Pekka Kaitaniemi wrote a theory study in PLOS ONE in 2008 on a neglected number in a common growth law. Allometric equations link a trait to body size with the form Y equals b times X to the power a. They are used across biology, from trees to animals, to scale one measure against another.

Most work focuses on the power a, while the constant b is treated as a mere scaling fix with no meaning. Kaitaniemi shows how real biological facts can be read out of b itself. If he is right, old data sets hold untapped facts, since b has been reported for decades and largely ignored.
plos-pone-0002032:
Matthias Habjan and co-authors showed how some viruses trim their genomes to hide from immunity, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Fast interferon release is the core of innate defense against viruses. Two sensors, RIG-I and MDA5, detect viral RNA by traits such as triple-phosphate ends or double strands, and set off that alarm.

Negative-strand RNA viruses carry genomes whose ends can bear those alarm traits. As the title states, processing the genome's five-prime ends is a strategy these viruses use to avoid RIG-I and the interferon call. Naming the dodge helps design viruses and vaccines that cannot hide.
plos-pone-0002132:
Roger Bate and co-authors bought malaria drugs from pharmacies across Africa and tested what was in them, for a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The team worked in the major cities of six African countries, in the part of the world where malaria hits hardest. They collected a range of antimalarial drugs from private drug shops in city and near-city areas.

Using thin-layer chromatography, a simple lab test that separates the parts of a mixture, they checked drug quality. Fake or weak malaria drugs cost lives, since patients trust pills that may hold too little of the active drug. The study gives hard data on a trade that thrives where checks are rare.
plos-pone-0002232:
Melissa Andrew, Arnold Mitnitski, and Kenneth Rockwood measured how social weakness relates to frailty and death in older people, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Social vulnerability covers things like living alone, low contact with others, and poor support. It is tied to the health of elderly people, but how to measure it, and how it relates to physical frailty, was disputed.

The authors built a social vulnerability index by counting deficits, the same approach used for frailty indexes. They then compared the two measures and their links to mortality. The study gives geriatric care a firmer way to count social risk alongside bodily risk.
plos-pone-0002332:
Selene Báez and Scott Collins tracked what happens when shrubs invade a desert grassland in New Mexico, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Climate change is shifting species ranges worldwide. As invading species enter a community, they alter who interacts with whom, which can reduce the stability that guards biodiversity. Arid lands are seeing this change fast.

In the northern Chihuahuan Desert, the team found shrub invasion decreases plant diversity and alters community stability. Fewer species and a shakier community make the ecosystem less able to absorb drought and other shocks. Their long look at one desert site gives measured weight to a pattern reported across dry regions.
plos-pone-0002432:
Research by Rao and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Srinivas Rao, Wing-Pui Kong, Chih-Jen Wei, and others. Its subject is multivalent HA DNA Vaccination Protects against Highly Pathogenic H5N1 Avian Influenza Infection in Chickens and Mice. Sustained outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 in avian species increase the risk of reassortment and adaptation to humans.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002532:
Hsiao and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Edward C. Hsiao, Yuko Yoshinaga, Trieu D. Nguyen, and others. Its subject is marking Embryonic Stem Cells with a 2A Self-Cleaving Peptide: A NKX2-5 Emerald GFP BAC Reporter. Fluorescent reporters are useful for assaying gene expression in living cells and for identifying and isolating pure cell populations from heterogeneous cultures.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002632:
Work by David Cohen and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was are child and adolescent responses to placebo higher in major depression than in anxiety disorders? a systematic review of Placebo-Controlled trials. The catalog record names David Cohen first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. In a previous report. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002732:
Work by Margarida Cunha-Rodrigues and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was Genistein-Supplemented diet decreases malaria liver infection in mice and constitutes a potential prophylactic strategy. Authorship is credited in the record to Margarida Cunha-Rodrigues and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. In tropical regions millions of people still live at risk of malaria infection. The authors add a further point. Indeed the emergence of resistance to chloroquine and other drugs in use in these areas reinforces the need to implement alternative prophylactic strategies. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. The full text can be read in the library, and this summary adds nothing beyond the record and abstract held for the entry.
plos-pone-0002832:
Work by Elina Mäntylä and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was from plants to birds: higher avian predation rates in trees responding to insect herbivory. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Elina Mäntylä, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. An understanding of the evolution of potential signals from plants to the predators of their herbivores may provide exciting examples of co-evolution among multiple. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002932:
Matt Finer, Clinton Jenkins, Stuart Pimm and co-authors mapped oil and gas threats in the western Amazon in 2008. That region is the richest part of the Amazon basin for wildlife and home to many indigenous groups. Some of the world's last uncontacted peoples live there in voluntary isolation.

Unlike the eastern Brazilian Amazon, the west was still largely intact at the time. The PLOS ONE paper sets out where energy projects press on wilderness, biodiversity, and indigenous peoples. Conservation planners get a region-wide picture of risk at a moment when choices could still protect large areas.
plos-pone-0003032:
Lorenzo Moroni, Doreen Hamann, Luca Paoluzzi and co-authors built scaffolds for joint tissue repair in 2008. Scaffolds for osteochondral engineering, covering bone plus cartilage, must be mechanically stable. They must also signal cells to regrow both tissues and offer a fully connected pore network for cell movement and growth.

Their approach converges technologies, combining polymer and ceramic composites toward that end, as the title phrases it. Published in PLOS ONE, regenerating articular tissue matters for joint injury and arthritis, where cartilage heals poorly on its own. Scaffold design is a main bottleneck. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003132:
Antonio G. Pacheco, Betina Durovni, Solange C. Cavalcante and colleagues study AIDS and tuberculosis together in Rio de Janeiro in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Brazil has offered free combined antiretroviral therapy to all since 1997, which sets the scene for the study. The team used past surveillance records at the population level.

They tracked how often tuberculosis, AIDS, AIDS deaths and combined AIDS-TB infection occurred in the city. Readers get a population view of two linked epidemics under free HIV treatment. The work helps judge where TB control in people with HIV still falls short.
plos-pone-0003232:
Yuki Sugiura, Shuichi Shimma, Yoshiyuki Konishi and colleagues apply imaging mass spectrometry to brain fats in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Gangliosides are particularly abundant in the central nervous system and are thought to play important roles in memory formation, nerve growth, synaptic transmission and other neural functions. Although several molecular species of gangliosides had been characterized, their exact distribution was less clear.

The authors visualize age-dependent accumulation of C20-ganglioside species in the mouse hippocampus, a memory region. Readers see chemistry mapped in place and across age. Spatial maps like this can link specific molecules to the brain regions they may affect.
plos-pone-0003332:
Carolina Rezával, Jimena Berni, Ezequiel Axel Gorostiza and colleagues screen for degeneration genes in flies in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Drosophila is a proven model to study the molecular basis of neurodegenerative diseases. The team carried out a misexpression screen to find genes involved in neurodegeneration. They examined locomotor behaviour in young and aged flies. They thought a progressive loss of function would appear with age.

Their screen uncovers a role for the gene Enabled in progressive neurodegeneration. Readers get a gene lead found by behaviour first, then biology. Fly screens remain a fast way to name genes for study in human brain disease.
plos-pone-0007432:
Ilmari Kurki, Tarja Peromaa, and Aapo Hyvärinen published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on why we judge brightness the way we do. Two patches can give the same reading on a light meter yet look clearly different. Perceived brightness depends on the spatial pattern of an image, not only on light levels. The usual assumption blamed the borders between light and dark areas.

The team used a method called classification images to reveal which features drive brightness judgments. Volunteers judged many noisy images, and the patterns behind their answers were extracted statistically. The results show that brightness perception rests on more than border analysis alone. Richer image structure shapes what people see. The findings refine how vision scientists model one of the most basic acts of seeing.
plos-pone-0007532:
Terry Smith and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the parasite that causes African sleeping sickness. Trypanosoma brucei coats itself in a dense layer of variant surface glycoprotein. That coat shields it from destruction by the host's complement system. The team blocked production of the coat using RNA interference. They then watched what happened inside the parasite.

Blocking coat synthesis triggered a general arrest in translation initiation. The parasite stopped starting new proteins across the board. The coat is so essential that the cell will not build without it. That coupling is a striking piece of quality control. It also suggests a vulnerability: attack the coat supply and the whole factory halts. The study reframes the parasite's famous disguise as a load-bearing wall.
plos-pone-0007632:
Jean-Fred Fontaine and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on improving gene-based diagnosis of thyroid lesions. Microarray tests measure the activity of many genes at once. Markers found this way for thyroid cancers had offered limited accuracy. The authors blamed the coarse categories usually used: too few classes of lesions were analyzed at once. They re-ran the analysis with more lesion classes included simultaneously.

With finer classes, the diagnostic markers became more relevant. Separating look-alike lesions lets each one's true signature emerge. A sharper test can spare patients needless surgery for benign growths. It can also catch cancers that coarse tests blur. The lesson reaches beyond the thyroid: category design shapes what gene tests can see. Sometimes the fix for a weak marker is a better question.
plos-pone-0007732:
Mourad Ferhat and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns Legionella pneumophila, the bacterium behind Legionnaires' disease. People catch it by breathing in contaminated mist. In nature, the bacterium lives inside free-living amoebas.

The authors studied a protein called TolC in the bacterium's outer membrane. TolC plays a major role in resistance to many drugs. It also matters in the early steps of invading a host. A single pump-like protein thus helps the germ both survive treatment and start infection. Blocking it could weaken the pathogen on two fronts.
plos-pone-0007832:
Erik van Lunteren and Michelle Moyer published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It profiles gene activity in the breathing muscle of diabetic rats. Diabetes weakens the diaphragm, the main muscle of breathing. Known causes include changed sugar and fat use, oxidative stress and altered membrane behavior.

The authors asked how much of that damage involves changed gene expression. They measured which genes turn up or down in the type 1 diabetes rat diaphragm. The profile shows the muscle's decline written in its genes. It may reveal new points where treatment could protect breathing in diabetes.
plos-pone-0007932:
Sandro Santagata and colleagues tested a marker for rare eye and brain tumors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The marker is CRX, a protein that helps keep retina and pineal cells true to their type. Tumors from those tissues are hard to sort by looks alone.

Staining tumor samples for CRX showed the protein marks cancers of retinal and pineal origin well. A clear stain can help pathologists name a tumor when other signs are mixed. Naming the tumor right guides care, so a trusty marker has real value for these uncommon cancers.
plos-pone-0008032:
James Jones and Marcel Salathe measured public fear in the first days of a new flu in PLOS ONE in 2009. A swine-origin H1N1 virus had just begun to spread worldwide, and news coverage was intense. Health teams needed to know how scared people were and what they were doing about it.

Surveys taken early caught anxiety levels and the steps people took, from hand washing to shunning crowds. Fear can help or harm in an outbreak: it drives care, but also panic buying and stigma. The early snapshot gives planners a base for wording advice that calms without dulling caution.
plos-pone-0008132:
Paolo Carrega and colleagues tested whether a patient's own killer cells can kill their own melanoma in PLOS ONE in 2009. Natural killer cells are built to destroy tumor cells, but most proof came from cells of strangers. A patient's own cells meeting their own tumor is the test that matters for therapy.

Some patients' killer cells did destroy their melanoma; others barely scratched it. The gap tracked with HLA types, the identity tags on cells, and with a group of killer cells called unlicensed. Knowing who carries able killers could guide cell therapy to those it can help.
plos-pone-0008232:
Dale Hedges and colleagues reported exome sequencing of a human family in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The exome is the small part of the genome that codes for proteins. Reading it requires capturing just those regions from a sample. New capture arrays had recently made that comprehensive capture possible. Efficient use of next-generation sequencing depended on such tools.

The team sequenced a multigenerational pedigree, a family tree spanning several generations. Family data help separate real inherited variants from noise. Their work showed exome sequencing could serve human genetics research in practice. It was an early step toward routine exome studies.
plos-pone-0008332:
Ludmil B. Alexandrov, Stoyana Alexandrova, and Anny Usheva modeled cells in altered gravity in PLOS ONE in 2009. How living systems respond to hostile environments is important but hard to study. Living systems are overwhelmingly complex for standard differential equations. Gravity changes are one such hostile factor for cultured cells. The team chose computer modeling as another way forward.

Their model describes gravity-related adaptation in cell cultures. Simulation can explore conditions that are costly to test in orbit or clinostats. Predictions from the model can then guide real experiments. The work applies computing to a problem in space biology.
plos-pone-0008432:
Warren Pilbrough, Trent Munro, and Peter Gray wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on CHO cells used to make drugs. CHO cells are lab cells from hamsters. Drug firms grow them to make proteins used as medicine. Picking a good cell line takes much time and money. Cells from the same clone can still make very unlike amounts of protein.

The authors study that spread within a clone. They ask why sister cells differ so much in what they make. Their findings bear on how firms screen and pick cell lines. More stable lines would make drug production faster and cheaper.
plos-pone-0008532:
Zhi-Xiang Xu and co-authors test a plant compound on cancer cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Avicin D belongs to the avicins, a family of plant triterpenoids. Avicins potently inhibit tumor cell growth. They also show antioxidant, anti-mutagenic, and anti-inflammatory actions. Prior work used Jurkat cells, a leukemia cell line. The team ask how Avicin D triggers apoptosis, the programmed death of cells.

They find Avicin D recruits Fas, a death receptor, into lipid rafts. Lipid rafts are ordered patches in the cell membrane. Downstream signaling molecules gather there too, starting the death cascade. That recruitment explains how a plant compound can kill tumor cells.
plos-pone-0008632:
Fengxia Liu and co-authors compare rice gene expression under stress in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Rice feeds more than half the world's population. Two major Asian subspecies are japonica and indica. They show significant phenotypic variation in stress responses. The molecular mechanisms behind that variation were unclear. The team profile gene expression in Nipponbare, a japonica variety, and 93-11, an indica variety, during oxidative stress.

Their profiles decipher which genes drive the differing responses. Some genes switch on in one subspecies but not the other. Those differences may explain why varieties tolerate stress unequally. Breeders can use the candidates to improve stress tolerance in rice.
plos-pone-0008732:
David Vandorpe, Chang Xu, Boris Shmukler, and colleagues studied why sickle red cells dry out. Their work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Red cells carrying sickle hemoglobin deform when oxygen runs low. Low oxygen opens an unknown leak that lets calcium flood in. Calcium then triggers potassium loss, and water follows. Dried cells stiffen and block small vessels.

The team characterized the leak in human and mouse sickle cells. Carbon monoxide and a spider-toxin peptide both dampened the current. Naming what controls the leak gives drug makers a target. Blocking it might keep sickle cells hydrated and flexible.
plos-pone-0008832:
Tomas Drgon, Ping-Wu Zhang, Catherine Johnson, and colleagues double-checked a genome-wide hunt for addiction genes. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Addiction risk is largely inherited but spread across many genes. Each gene contributes only a small share. Genome-wide scans without templates offer one way to find them. A second analytic style offered an independent check.

Results that replicated across both approaches carry more trust. The comparison also exposes where methods disagree and why. Addiction genetics needs such cross-checks before claims harden. The work steadies a field prone to false leads.
plos-pone-0008932:
Jacob Nabe-Nielsen and co-authors modelled what happens to wild animals when people reshape the land, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Roads, farms, and towns split wild habitat into smaller pieces. Managers need to know whether a population can survive such changes for decades. Real experiments on whole landscapes are almost impossible to run.

The team built computer landscapes and let virtual animals live, breed, and die in them. They then altered the land and watched which populations held on or faded out. Small changes in movement or breeding success could decide survival over the long run. The model gives planners a way to test land changes before making them.
plos-pone-0009032:
Maureen Donlin and co-authors asked whether the hepatitis C virus's own genes shape treatment success, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hepatitis C comes in six major genotypes. Patients with genotype 1 answer interferon therapy worse than others. African American patients respond only about half as often as Caucasian American patients.

The team compared whole viral genomes from patients of both groups. Differences scattered across the virus, not just in known hotspots, mattered. Viral genetics helped explain who cleared the virus on interferon. Reading the virus's genome could one day guide treatment choices for each patient.
plos-pone-0009132:
Orit Uziel and co-authors shortened cancer cells' chromosome caps to make drugs bite harder, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Telomeres cap the ends of chromosomes and shrink as cells divide. Telomerase rebuilds them, and most cancers switch it back on to keep growing. Blocking this enzyme makes tumours shrink and sensitises them to many drugs.

The team asked whether the shortening itself does the sensitising work. Cells with shortened telomeres died more readily under chosen cytotoxic agents. The effect held in lab dishes and in tumours in animals alike. Pairing a telomere attack with standard chemotherapy could strengthen both treatments.
plos-pone-0009232:
Christian Denecke and co-authors published this transplant study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Older patients are a fast-growing group on organ waiting lists. Age changes the immune system, and that changes how a transplant is attacked or tolerated. The team compared T cell behavior in young and old mice.

Using both normal and transgenic mouse transplant models, they tested effector and regulatory T cells. Grafts lasted longer in older recipients. The reason was weaker attack from effector T cells, while regulatory T cells still did their calming job. That imbalance suggests older patients might need gentler anti-rejection treatment than younger ones.
plos-pone-0009332:
Jack Nguyen and co-authors published this flu drug study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The 2009 H1N1 flu spread worldwide and was declared the first pandemic of the century. At the same time, flu strains were growing resistant to single drugs. A resistant virus can render a whole medicine cabinet useless.

The team tested three flu drugs together: amantadine, ribavirin, and oseltamivir. In lab dishes, the triple mix was highly active against drug-resistant strains. The drugs also boosted each other, an effect called synergy. Combining drugs makes resistance harder, because the virus must escape all three at once.
plos-pone-0011432:
Marin Schweizer and co-authors reviewed hospital records in 2010 to test a routine habit in severe infection care. When Staphylococcus aureus enters the blood, doctors start antibiotics at once, before lab results name the exact strain, a practice called empiric therapy. The assumption is that an early, best-guess drug saves lives compared with waiting.

In their retrospective cohort, patients who got empiric therapy did not show lower death rates in the hospital than those who did not. That sobering result does not prove early treatment is useless, but it challenges a reflex habit in one of medicine's nastiest bloodstream infections. Hospitals reading the study are pushed to check their own data and to ask which patients, if any, truly gain from the early guess.
plos-pone-0011632:
Robert Pool and colleagues checked the reliability of trial data in the MDP301 vaginal microbicide trial, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Such HIV prevention trials depend on honest reports of gel use and sexual behaviour. No gold standard exists, so reports are usually taken on trust.

The team applied the Microbicides Development Programme's mixed methods model, cross-checking different data sources against each other. Their assessment shows where self-reports hold up and where they drift. Trialists can use the verdict to correct results and to design future studies that catch reporting errors before they distort conclusions.
plos-pone-0011732:
Shan-xue Jin and Larry Feig traced a memory pathway in the rat hippocampus, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Long-term potentiation, a lasting strengthening of synapses, is a leading model of how learning is stored. Receptors called NMDA receptors are major contributors, and a version containing the NR2A subunit had been the focus of most prior work.

Jin and Feig showed that potentiation driven by those receptors in the CA1 region runs through Ras-GRF2 and the Erk MAP kinase relay. Detailing this route from synapse to lasting change refines the molecular account of how memories may form.
plos-pone-0011932:
Joaquín Muñoz and colleagues traced in 2010 the history of a brine shrimp that reproduces without males. Artemia parthenogenetica is an obligate parthenogen, meaning females produce daughters without fertilization. Studying where such lineages come from bears on a big question: why sexual reproduction persists at all.

The team assessed the lineage's geographic origin, genetic diversity, and spread across its range. A clone-like animal that has traveled widely is a natural experiment in how far asexual life can go. Its history shows both the reach and the limits of skipping sex, since the lineage's diversity records every mutation it has gathered since its birth.
plos-pone-0012032:
Joern Kuhbier and co-workers tested in 2010 whether spider silk can serve as a scaffold for growing tissue. Tissue engineering needs matrices for cells to live on, and silk's strength and fineness make it a candidate. Silkworm silk can provoke immune reactions, pushing interest toward spider silk instead.

The team seeded NIH/3T3 fibroblasts, standard connective tissue cells, onto miniature weaving frames holding spider silk, then studied how the cells interacted with the fibers. Whether cells attach, spread, and thrive on silk decides if the material has a future in implants. Hand-built frames let the team test real woven silk rather than silk dissolved into films.
plos-pone-0012132:
Mathew Cox, Murray Cairns, Kaushal Gandhi, and co-authors studied small RNAs in the blood of people with multiple sclerosis, in PLOS ONE in 2010. This disease turns the immune system against the nerves, yet what loosens the immune system's normal controls is still unclear. Small RNAs called microRNAs act as dimmers on genes, and two of them were known to restrain genes that switch T cells on.

In blood from patients, those two microRNAs were present at lower levels than in healthy people. Looser dimmers could let T cell activation genes run hotter, fitting the disease's immune attack. The finding names candidate markers in an easy-to-sample tissue and new suspects in the search for what drives the illness.
plos-pone-0012232:
Christine Waasdorp Hurtado, Lucy Golden-Mason, Megan Brocato, and co-authors studied newborns of mothers with hepatitis C, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most childhood hepatitis C comes from infection around birth, yet strikingly few exposed babies actually catch the virus, while most infected adults stay infected for life. Something in the newborn's first defenses seems to hold the virus off more often than chance would allow.

The team examined the built-in, fast arm of immunity in placentas and cord blood from infected mothers and their infants. Finding what protects most babies could point to vaccine ideas or treatments for everyone. It is a case where the exception, resistance, teaches more than the rule.
plos-pone-0012332:
Maria Wilbe, Martine Lund Ziener, Anita Aronsson, and co-authors linked immune genes to a claw disease of dogs, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Symmetrical lupoid onychodystrophy destroys the claws of otherwise healthy dogs, and its pattern suggests the immune system attacking the claw bed by mistake. The team typed the dog version of the immune identity genes, the DLA class II set, in ninety-eight affected Gordon setters and compared them with controls.

Certain alleles of those genes tracked with higher risk of the disease. A genetic risk map lets breeders lower the disease's frequency over generations without losing the breed's other traits. It also confirms the autoimmune theory, pointing treatment toward immune-calming approaches.
plos-pone-0012432:
Steven Boyden and Louis Kunkel scanned the genomes of long-lived families for shared DNA regions, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. About a quarter of human lifespan runs in families, and genes may matter most for the rare people who pass ninety in good health. Siblings of centenarians live far longer than average, a strong hint of protective genes.

Using dense genome-wide linkage in families with exceptional longevity, the team found several new regions tied to long life. Each region is a haystack with candidate genes inside. Finding true longevity genes could reveal how some bodies resist age diseases and suggest ways to extend healthy years for everyone.
plos-pone-0012532:
Piotr Grabarczyk, Viola Nähse, Martin Delin and colleagues raised a gene regulator in cancer cells and tested drug response, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Bcl11b is a transcription factor found in T cells, neurons, and skin, and its locus is often disturbed in blood cancers. What extra Bcl11b does to a cell's drug sensitivity was unknown.

Cells with more Bcl11b resisted chemotherapy and piled up in the G1 phase of the cell cycle, the waiting stage before DNA copying. Slow-cycling cells often survive drugs aimed at dividing ones. The finding warns that this regulator's level could mark tumors likely to shrug off standard treatment.
plos-pone-0012632:
Sjoholm, Backlund and co-authors linked a clock gene to the fastest form of bipolar disorder. People with bipolar disorder often have broken sleep and daily rhythms. The gene CRY2 helps run the body's inner clock, and its activity in blood cells was known to change with mood state.

Their 2010 study compared patients whose moods cycle rapidly with others, looking for CRY2 differences. A link would tie rapid cycling to the clock machinery itself, not just to symptoms. That could guide treatments that steady daily rhythms, such as light and sleep routines.
plos-pone-0012732:
Henry, Blank, Hoose and co-authors separated two jobs of the cell's protein stress response in yeast. When proteins fold badly in the cell's workshop, the unfolded protein response raises the alarm. Their 2010 study used baker's yeast to test whether that response is needed for cells to enter division.

They found it is not required for the move into DNA copying, but it is required to keep chromosomes intact. Splitting those roles clarifies what the alarm is really for. Chromosome care links this basic pathway to cancer and ageing research.
plos-pone-0012832:
Osterblom, Sumaila, Bodin and co-authors argued that illegal fishing fleets move to wherever enforcement is weakest. Illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing drains fish stocks and harms sea ecosystems. Their 2010 paper frames this as a governance problem that shifts across regions rather than a fixed map of bad actors.

As some regions tighten control, effort slides toward places with a lower governance score. Chasing that slide needs joint action across countries, not port-by-port fixes. The paper gives managers a dynamic picture of the problem instead of a static one.
pmc-4779832:
Zhang, Wang, Vikash, and their colleagues reviewed reactive oxygen species signaling in 2016. Reactive oxygen species, or ROS, are reactive molecules made in cells. It has long been known that a rise in ROS can modify signaling proteins and change what cells do.

The review traces how ROS-mediated signaling works in healthy cells and how it can go wrong. Excess ROS is tied to diseases such as atherosclerosis, diabetes, unchecked growth, and degeneration of nerves, plus inflammation. Cells also use controlled ROS as messengers, so the balance matters. Understanding that balance guides antioxidant and signaling research.
pmc-7402632:
Jérémie Hadjadj and colleagues reported in 2020 that patients with severe COVID-19 share a telling immune weakness. Interferons are the body's first alarm proteins against viruses, and type I interferons switch on a battery of antiviral genes. In these severely ill patients, that alarm was unusually faint, while inflammation elsewhere in the body ran high.

The team measured interferon activity and inflammatory signals in patients across levels of illness severity. The pairing they found, weak antiviral defense beside strong inflammation, helps explain why the virus can gain ground while the body's response still damages tissue. Their report pointed toward treatments that might restore the early alarm or calm the late inflammation, and it shaped how doctors thought about timing immune therapies.
pmc-8096432:
Francesco Beghini and colleagues introduced bioBakery 3 in 2021, a set of tools for profiling microbial communities in depth. Shotgun metagenomics reads all the DNA in a sample, letting researchers ask which microbes are present and what they can do. The new version extends profiling beyond species lists to the functions microbes carry and even to individual strains.

The authors describe how the tools integrate taxonomic, functional, and strain level views of the same community. They show the system working across varied sample types and studies. Distinguishing strains matters because two microbes of one species can behave very differently, and the update brought that finer resolution into a widely used workflow.
pmc-8995832:
Willem de Vos, Herbert Tilg, and colleagues reviewed in 2022 the mechanisms by which the gut microbiome shapes human health. The community of microbes in the gut is now counted among the key regulators of the body's condition. Nearly every body site carries its own microbes, each in conversation with the organs nearby.

Drawing on newer molecular tools, the authors explain how gut microbes influence immunity, metabolism, and even the brain, and how those influences can turn harmful. They survey the pathways involved, from the chemicals microbes produce to their effects on the gut wall. The review offers a mechanism level account for readers who want more than the claim that the microbiome matters.
plos-pone-0360432:
Yirui Jiang and colleagues proposed in 2026 a method for sorting city patrol cases by how urgent they are. Patrol and municipal hotline systems receive a flood of reports, from broken streetlights to active hazards, and staff must decide what to handle first. Their method uses a graph neural network, a model that learns from cases and the connections between them, trained with self-supervised clustering so it needs few hand labeled examples.

Sorting by urgency sounds clerical, but it decides how fast real dangers get attention in a big city. An automated first pass, checked by humans, can keep urgent cases from waiting behind routine ones. The study belongs to a wider effort to bring machine learning into everyday city administration.
plos-pone-0358132:
Kaothar Lambe and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on malaria in sub-Saharan Africa. It follows Plasmodium falciparum histidine-rich protein 2, a protein that many rapid malaria tests detect. The authors study its spatial and genetic dynamics, how the protein's gene varies across places and over populations.

Changes or deletions in this gene can make rapid tests miss infections, a serious threat where those tests are the main diagnostic. Mapping the gene's geography shows where test failure risk is highest. Malaria control programs across Africa rely on this surveillance to decide when to switch diagnostic tools.
plos-pone-0359632: Lim and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE survey study on advance care planning. Such planning lets people state the care they want if they become too ill to decide. The team asked patients how they feel about it and what shapes whether talks happen. A questionnaire design captured views at one point in time. The answers can help clinics start these talks sooner and more gently.
plos-pone-0359232: Kim and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a balloon used to reopen narrowed heart arteries. The balloon carries a drug coating and a fine surface pattern of tiny structures. In pigs with re-narrowed stents, the title reports stronger early biological effect from the patterned balloon. Re-narrowing after stenting is a stubborn problem, so coating design draws wide interest.
europmc-pmc7347232: Published in 2020, this research paper takes on the genome polishing tool POLCA makes fast and accurate fixes in genome assemblies. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. A tested new tool like this gives doctors a steadier way to measure what they see in patients.
europmc-pmc8063132: A fresh look at maternal and neonatal sickness and deaths among pregnant women with and without COVID-19 infection: the INTERCOVID multinational cohort study arrived with this 2021 research paper. Importance detailed information about the link of COVID-19 with results in pregnant individuals compared with not-infected pregnant individuals is much. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
gao-gaoreports-b-310732: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by PMC Solutions, Inc. Decided January 22, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
europmc-pmc7574532: This 2020 research paper covers living risk forecasting algorithm for risk of hospital admission and deaths from COVID-19 in adults: national derivation and validation cohort. To derive and validate a risk forecasting algorithm to estimate hospital admission and deaths results from COVID-19 (COVID-19) in adults. Better ways to spot trouble early give doctors a head start on treatment.
europmc-pmc9280632: Published in 2022, this research paper takes on shaping polarization of tumor-linked macrophages (immune cleanup cells) in cancer immunotherapy (treatment that boosts the immune system). The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc7266132: A fresh look at the gut microbiome (microbes living in the body)'s role in the growth, maintenance, and results of sepsis (a body-wide infection crisis) arrived with this 2020 research paper. The gut microbiome (microbes living in the body) controls a number of homeostatic mechanisms (the inner workings) in the healthy. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9402432: Mishima and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on a non-canonical vitamin k cycle is a potent ferroptosis (an iron-driven form of cell death) suppressor. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc7904932: A fresh look at genome-wide (across all DNA) meta-analysis (a study pooling many studies) identifies 127 open-angle glaucoma loci with consistent effect across ancestries arrived with this 2021 research paper. Primary open-angle glaucoma, is a heritable common cause of blindness world-wide. A good review shows what is solid, what is shaky, and where the next study should look.
europmc-pmc7911532: A 2021 review paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at COVID-19: a review on the COVID-19 disease evolution (gradual change), spread, spotting, control and prevention (keeping illness away). The authors pull together the key findings from across the field. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc8995832: de and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on gut microbiome (microbes living in the body) and health: mechanistic insights. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8076232: Doctors and scientists took on achieving clinical (in patients) success with BET blockers as anti-cancer agents in this 2021 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc7017232: Published in 2020, this research paper takes on aimed at aberrant RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK signaling (cell-to-cell messaging) for cancer therapy. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
europmc-pmc7187532: A 2020 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at circatlas: an integrated resource of one million highly accurate circular rnas from 1070 vertebrate transcriptomes. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc7916132: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on survey of MMP-13 as a promising target for the treatment of osteoarthritis. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc7205032: Doctors and scientists took on COVID-19 and the 5G conspiracy theory: social network analysis of twitter data in this 2020 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8786632: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at multiple early factors anticipate post-acute COVID-19 sequelae. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc7523332: A 2020 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at single-cell (one cell at a time) transcriptome analysis of tumor and stromal compartments of of the pancreas ductal adenocarcinoma primary tumors. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8081532: A 2021 review paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at slows and disruptions in cancer health care due to COVID-19 pandemic: systematic review (a review of every study). It pulls together all the available studies on the question and grades the evidence. A good review shows what is solid, what is shaky, and where the next study should look.
europmc-pmc8707132: Doctors and scientists took on linked factors of sarcopenia in community-dwelling older adults: a systematic review (a review of every study) in this 2021 research paper. The team pooled the numbers from many earlier studies into one stronger result. Having the evidence weighed in one place saves busy doctors from sifting through dozens of papers alone.
europmc-pmc9052532: Doctors and scientists took on gut microbiota (the microbes living in the body) influence immunotherapy (treatment that boosts the immune system) replies: mechanisms (the inner workings) in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
europmc-pmc7402632: This 2020 research paper covers impaired type i interferon (virus-fighting protein) action and inflammatory (swelling-related) replies in severe COVID-19 patients. COVID-19 is characterized by distinct patterns of disease progression (worsening) that suggest diverse host immune responses (the immune system's replies). Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc7239332: Dbouk and co-authors published this research paper in 2020 on on coughing and airborne droplet spread to humans. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8234032: This 2021 research paper covers recent advances (new steps forward) in tumor aimed at via EPR effect for cancer treatment. Cancer causes the second-highest rate of death world-wide. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc7351732: A fresh look at control of cancer cell metabolism (how cells turn food into energy): oncogenic MYC in the driver's seat arrived with this 2020 research paper. Cancer cells must rewire of cells metabolism (how cells turn food into energy) to satisfy the demands of unbridled growth. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8158032: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on gut akkermansia muciniphila eases metabolic (energy-use) dysfunction-linked fatty liver disease by regulating the metabolism (how cells turn food into energy). The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
europmc-pmc8967832: Kim and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on tissue extracellular (outside cells) matrix hydrogels as alternatives to matrigel for culturing gastrointestinal organoids. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc7145632: Published in 2020, this research paper takes on mgnify: the microbiome (microbes living in the body) analysis resource in 2020. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9033932: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at aimed at tgf-β signal transduction for fibrosis (scarring of tissue) and cancer therapy. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc9869432: Li and co-authors published this research paper in 2023 on protein-to-genome alignment with miniprot. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.

Deaths statistics are fundamental to public health decision making. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.

europmc-pmc7045432: A fresh look at m6a demethylase ALKBH5 blocks tumor growth and metastasis (cancer spread) by reducing ythdfs-driven YAP expression (gene activity) and inhibiting mir-107/lats2-driven YAP acti arrived with this 2020 research paper. europmc-pmc8218332: A fresh look at reduced neutralization of SARS-CoV-2 b-1-617 by vaccine and convalescent serum arrived with this 2021 research paper. europmc-pmc7464532: Zielińska and co-authors published this research paper in 2020 on polymeric nanoparticles (ultra-tiny specks): production, characterization (detailed description), toxicology and ecotoxicology. europmc-pmc7794332: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on gut microbiota (the microbes living in the body) impact on the peripheral immune response (the immune system's reply) in non-alcoholic fatty liver. europmc-pmc7504732: This 2020 research paper covers chitosan: a natural biopolymer with a wide and varied range of uses. Although chitin is of the most available biopolymers on earth its uses and uses are limited due. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8096432: A fresh look at integrating taxonomic, working, and strain-level profiling of diverse germ communities with biobakery 3 arrived with this 2021 research paper. Culture-independent analyses of germ communities have progressed dramatically in the last decade, particularly due to advances (new steps forward). To fully utilize the advances (new steps forward) in omics technologies and achieve a more thorough understanding (grasp of). europmc-pmc9281132: This 2022 research paper covers wnt signaling (cell-to-cell messaging) in colorectal (of the colon and rectum) cancer: pathogenic role and treatment target. gao-gaoreports-b-311332: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Corcel Corporation. Decided June 13, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. gao-gaoreports-gao-08-432: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on grants Management: Attention Needed to Address Undisbursed Balances in Expired Grant Accounts. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
europmc-pmc8791832: Doctors and scientists took on human blastoids model blastocyst growth and implantation in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-732: GAO published its findings on compact of Free Association: Palau's Use of and Accountability for US Assistance and Prospects for Economic Self-Sufficiency in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
europmc-pmc7272632: A fresh look at liquid-liquid phase separation triggers pathogenic tau conformations in vitro (in lab dishes) arrived with this 2020 research paper. Formation of membrane-less organelles via liquid-liquid phase separation is one way cells meet the biological (from living things) requirement. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8890532: Zhang and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on the role of mitochondrial (tied to the cell's energy plants) reactive oxygen species in homeostasis control. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
europmc-pmc7870932: A fresh look at biallelic loss of BCMA as a resistance mechanism (how it works) to CAR t cell therapy in a patient arrived with this 2021 research paper. BCMA aimed at chimeric antigen receptor (docking point on a cell) t cell therapy has shown deep and durable replies. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
ballads-pg2732: Thackeray's ballads: his comic and sentimental verses. "The Age of Wisdom" and others, witty and tuneful. The satirist as poet. Thackeray's verse is wit set to music, the satirist sings, the satirist sings his comic songs.
in-the-wilderness-pg3132: Charles Dudley Warner's In the Wilderness: Adirondack sketches. The camper's classic, fresh and true. The woods' own book. Adirondack sketches, fresh and true, the camper's classic, the woods' book, Adirondack sketches, the woods’ own book.
plos-pone-0358332:
Masaru Shirasuna and Yuto Yoshida compare how trivia champions and large language models read a quiz question, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Human experts often buzz in with the answer after only a few words, working from far less knowledge than a model holds. The authors had both the experts and language models rate the importance of every word in Japanese quiz questions, using the models themselves as judging tools.

Experts spread their attention widely, treating many words as useful clues even when each looked weakly tied to the answer on its own. Their importance scores also piled up faster as a question unfolded. The models, by contrast, concentrated on fewer, more obviously connected words. The authors read the pattern as a hint about human intelligence under time pressure: experts may weave many faint signals together rather than waiting for one decisive hint.
plos-pone-0356632:
Maria Lamarca leads a team of eight asking whether men and women benefit equally from a psychological therapy for psychosis, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Metacognitive training teaches patients to spot the thinking shortcuts that feed delusions and suspicion. Sex shapes how schizophrenia begins and presents, so a fair question is whether one therapy fits both. The team pooled harmonized records from an international consortium, covering five hundred seventy-three patients treated in real clinics and studies.

Symptoms of every kind, positive, negative, and general, fell significantly after training across the whole group. Crucially, sex did not moderate the change: men and women improved comparably in every symptom domain, even though their starting profiles differed. With no control group, the data cannot prove the training itself caused the gains. But as far as equity goes, the therapy appears to travel across sexes without adjustment, a useful reassurance for routine services.
plos-pone-0357232:
Amani Abdallah Hepautwa leads a team of five baking waste into better bricks, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The recipe starts with burnt red soil and a swelling clay additive. Into it goes biochar, made by roasting coffee grounds or tobacco waste at three temperatures. The biochar replaces five to twenty percent of the mix. The team fired the bricks and measured strength three ways, resistance to water and chemical attack, and the microscopic structure behind the numbers.

Everything mattered: the waste type, the roasting temperature, and the dose all significantly shifted performance. One recipe won outright, coffee biochar roasted at the middle temperature and used at ten percent. It delivered the best balance of compressive, tensile, and bending strength in the study. The work gives brick makers in agricultural regions a tested way to convert two troublesome waste streams into a building material that outperforms the plain article.
plos-pone-0358232:
Vincent C T Hanlon led a team of eight authors testing an idea about a crop pest's genes, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Potato cyst nematodes devastate potato crops, and their HYP1 gene varies a lot between individuals. One theory held that the variation arises from programmed changes in body cells during development.

Hanlon's team tested that theory and found it does not explain the diversity at HYP1. Ruling out a mechanism is real progress: it narrows the hunt for where the variation truly comes from. Pest control may one day target this gene's variability, since it may help the worm evade plant defenses. Knowing what does not cause it saves other teams years of work in the wrong direction.
plos-pone-0355932:
Teshome Kabeta Dadi and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on what shapes rural Ethiopian women's say over farm and household decisions. Autonomy is tangled: age, schooling, wealth, religion, and cultural norms all pull at once, and effects differ between groups of women. Using survey data from nine rural districts, the team fitted a statistical tree model splitting women into segments by marital status and household headship, finding which factors matter in each.

Among married women in male-led households, autonomy rose with age, wealth, and joining social groups, and varied with religion and views of cultural gender norms. Unmarried women in male-led households showed the same pattern. In female-led households, fewer factors mattered: age and religious affiliation carried the signal. Programs, they advise, should work the levers that actually move each segment, cultural norms and social groups included, rather than treating rural women as one audience.
plos-pone-0357032:
Ahmed Saad AL Zomia and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE charting three decades of blindness and visual impairment across the six Gulf countries, with forecasts to 2030. Using Global Burden of Disease data, prevalence and disability burden were modeled with time-series methods, country by country and by sex.

Most countries improved. Prevalence edged down in Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, barely moved in Kuwait, and stayed broadly stable in Oman and Qatar. Disability burden fell across the region, though Saudi Arabia carried the heaviest load. Women bore higher prevalence than men almost everywhere, the Emirates being the exception. Forecasts point to continued declines in most countries through 2030, but a moderate rise in Oman. Gender-sensitive eye care and stronger infrastructure are urged: the Gulf's gains are real but uneven, and Oman needs attention before its trend turns.
plos-pone-0357832:
Talyson Aparício Gomes and coauthors published a 2026 qualitative study in PLOS ONE on patients who effectively live in a hospital, a tropical diseases referral center in Manaus, in the Brazilian Amazon. Some stays stretch past six months not because treatment continues, but because there is nowhere to discharge to. The team interviewed ten professionals working at the hospital and eight relatives of long-stay patients.

Five themes emerged, led by social hospitalization and institutional dependence. The cases overlapped heavily: chronic conditions, often HIV, fragile family ties, and deep poverty. Stigma around HIV and families' inability to afford home care blocked discharge, so the hospital became housing, community, and safety net at once. Caregivers' lives bent around the routine, and clinicians described obstacles no treatment plan could fix. Without intermediate care institutions and real policy, they conclude, tertiary hospitals will keep serving as the address of last resort.
plos-pone-0339732:
Mustafa Tunc runs flume experiments on how sand and gravel beds in straight channels reshape under flowing water. Two features matter for engineers: how deep the flow digs local holes and how high it piles dune crests. Working with three grain sizes, Tunc measured bed shapes across flow rates and built prediction formulas from the results.

Stronger flow raised both digging depth and dune height in every case. Fine grains shifted easily into regular dunes, while the coarsest grains armored the bed and held it stable; middle grains formed a mixed pattern of holes and bars. The formulas predicted both measures with high accuracy. Tunc presents them for designing channels and structures that must survive moving riverbeds.
plos-pone-0352132:
Saima Hirani and colleagues present a protocol, published in 2026, for the first review mapping research on postpartum mental health among racialized mothers in Canada. Nearly a quarter of Canadian mothers report depression or anxiety symptoms after birth. The authors note that mothers from racialized communities can face added stigma and discrimination. They can also face care that does not fit their culture.

The planned review will search four major databases plus grey literature for Canadian studies and programs. It will screen them in duplicate. It will chart themes rather than pooling statistics. Programs and interventions will be catalogued alongside research findings. The resulting map is meant to guide culturally responsive services. It should also show researchers exactly where evidence about these mothers is missing.
plos-pone-0344932:
Macy Garrood and colleagues present a method for putting whole fixed human brains into deep freeze for the long term. It is an alternative to storing them in jars of fluid. Fluid storage slowly degrades some molecules researchers care about. Their 2026 protocol gradually loads brains with cryoprotectants. It ends in a strong ethylene glycol and sucrose bath, then stores them below zero.

Patience is the catch. Scans showed the protectant needs roughly nine months to fully penetrate a whole brain. An early validation run froze too soon, leaving ice crystal damage in white matter. With the longer soak, microscopy showed cells and fine structure preserved. Brain banks weighing decades-long archives now have a tested freezing recipe.
plos-pone-0355232:
Nurlan Smagulov and five colleagues examine what years of teaching do to the body and mind, in a 2026 study of female secondary school teachers in Karaganda, Kazakhstan. Teaching is known to be draining, but researchers rarely separate the effects of simply growing older from the effects of a long career. The team measured heart rhythms, blood pressure, fitness, mood, anxiety, and attention in just over one hundred teachers.

Age and years of service were so closely tied that teasing them apart proved difficult. Still, career length was linked to a wider set of measures than age alone, including physical work capacity and emotional reactivity alongside blood pressure and self-rated well-being. The findings suggest that a long teaching career leaves its own mark beyond aging, a point schools could use when planning health support.
plos-pone-0355332: Bio-electrochemical reactors can strip organic carbon from wastewater — especially with nanoparticle help. This paper studied multi-phase reactions for organic carbon removal using Fe2O3-synthesized nanoparticles. The nanoparticle-enhanced process points toward cheaper, greener wastewater treatment.
plos-pone-0351932:
Xiaolin Tang and seven colleagues build a smarter safety check for intravenous nutrition bags prepared for newborns, in this 2026 hospital study. Ready-to-use nutrition for fragile infants must contain exactly what the prescription says; small errors matter at small body weights. Their system computes each bag's expected weight from drug densities held in the hospital computer, then compares it with a precision scale reading, replacing a slower method based on leftover liquid.

Across several hundred bags prepared by seven technicians, the weighing method proved precise and stable between operators, with nearly all error rates inside the preset limits. It also worked almost twice as fast per bag and caught several faulty infusions the older method missed. The authors recommend the system for pharmacy compounding centers preparing neonatal nutrition.
plos-pone-0353932:
