Lisa Van Wilder and five colleagues publish the protocol for a Belgian study of whether structured support helps teenagers with chronic illness move safely into adult care, in 2026. The transfer from pediatric to adult services is a known cliff edge where young patients drop out and health suffers. Their program, co-designed with patients, offers four structured consultations over more than a year, building readiness, autonomy, and continuity.

Two university hospitals will run a pretest-posttest comparison enrolling seventeen- and eighteen-year-olds with type 1 diabetes, asthma, or obesity into the program or usual care. Readiness is the main outcome, with empowerment, medication adherence, quality of life, and mental health also tracked, plus a cost-effectiveness analysis and a close look at how faithfully the program is delivered. The authors aim to inform both a refined program and a future large-scale trial.
plos-pone-0355832:
Lucas Pietan and colleagues hunted for genes behind the loss of smell and taste that many COVID-19 patients report. These symptoms can linger, and their biology is still partly unclear. Their 2026 study applied machine learning to genome data from two American patient cohorts of different sizes.

The team built a pipeline that ranks genes and variants by how well they separate patients with sensory loss. Best models sorted patients moderately well on held-out data. The shortlist mixed new candidates with known factors tied to immune response, nerve signalling, and calcium signalling. Pietan and colleagues say the results support earlier ideas about how the virus disturbs smell and taste, and they offer targets for follow-up.
plos-pone-0345032:
Naveed Sattar and colleagues re-analysed major obesity trials to see how often a weekly injection hits three health targets at once. Tirzepatide had already produced large weight losses in the SURMOUNT programme, in people with and without diabetes. Their 2026 post-hoc analysis counted patients reaching weight, blood pressure, and cholesterol goals together.

About a third of treated patients hit all three targets at the main weight-loss threshold, against only a small share on placebo. Results were similar when the weight bar was raised. Sattar and colleagues argue the combined endpoint matters because heart risk travels in clusters. Meeting weight, pressure, and cholesterol goals together marks fuller benefit than weight loss alone.
plos-pone-0335832:
Selin Kankaya and co-authors compared gene silencing marks in stomach cancer and in stomach inflammation tied to a common bacterium. The tumour suppressor gene in question is often switched off by methylation, a chemical tag, during cancer development. Whether the tag appears early, in Helicobacter-related gastritis, was unclear. Their 2026 study sampled tumours, inflamed tissue with and without the bacterium, and healthy lining.

Methylation ran far higher in cancer than in uninfected gastritis or healthy tissue. Strikingly, infected gastritis matched cancer levels and exceeded uninfected gastritis. The tag separated cancer from non-cancer fairly well, but poorly from infected gastritis. Protein levels did not differ across groups. Kankaya and colleagues caution the mark alone cannot flag cancer where infection is common.
plos-pone-0353232:
Olga Gorodetskaya and co-authors asked whether landing tenure changes when academics have children. Research usually runs the other way, asking how parenthood dents careers. Their 2026 study used a large original survey of Italian academics and tracked moves into first and second parenthood over time.

Job stability did open the door to parenthood. Tenure raised the chance of a first child for men, and for women who won it before their mid-thirties. Among childless women, tenure also raised short-term plans for a child. Tenure showed no link with second births for either sex. Gorodetskaya and colleagues say secure posts shape family timing, not only family shaping careers.
plos-pone-0343832:
Zehua Liu and colleagues present in 2026 a self service drone photo system built for visitors at cultural sites. Their aim was to remove the need for a licensed pilot on each order and to cut waits that once ran to days. The system splits work into small linked services that handle orders, drone choice, flight control, and video making.

In tests with many simulated users, core responses stayed fast and errors stayed very low. Cost per order fell sharply and delivery shrank to well under an hour. Fault tests caused no full outage. The authors offer the design as a model for other low altitude visitor services.
plos-pone-0355732:
Holly Edward and colleagues gather in 2026 expert views across Canada on a new guide role for physiotherapists in acute cancer care. A physiotherapist navigator would assess patients early, sort who needs what, and steer care. Two survey rounds plus a final meeting shaped the role, with set thresholds for agreement among health workers who treat cancer patients.

Agreement was reached on four parts: process, assessment, sorting decisions, and duties. Feedback lengthened appointments, spaced follow-ups, allowed self referral, and added objective tests. Respondents rated the role's usefulness very highly. A future trial will test whether the agreed design helps patients in real clinics.
plos-pone-0354232:
Malou Masereel and six colleagues published this 2026 study protocol for treating adults with avoidant and restrictive food intake disorder, a pattern of severely limited eating not driven by body image. No proven treatment exists yet. Their plan, run across eleven Dutch centers, gives about a hundred and twenty patients weekly therapy built on gradual exposure to feared foods.

Severity interviews anchor the checks before treatment, after it, and months later, while session notes track fear and expectations. Because there is no comparison group, Masereel presents the trial as groundwork for later controlled studies and sharper therapy design.
plos-pone-0354132:
Yasmine Wazzani and five colleagues published this 2026 field study of mint plants and the microbes living around their roots. Three closely related mint types grew side by side in the same soil, letting the team compare root-zone bacteria and fungi against soil chemistry and each plant's essential oil blend.

Each mint hosted a distinct microbial community, tied to both its oil chemistry and the surrounding soil. Root fungi that help plants feed were also measured. Wazzani's results show that even near-identical crops shape their own underground partners, a factor growers of medicinal herbs may learn to manage.
plos-pone-0351332:
Adrianne Katrina Nelson led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of deaths inside Los Angeles County jails from 2008 to 2023. Linking custody and death records for the biggest jail system in America, they examined how long people had been confined before dying, and how overdose and COVID-19 figured in.

Deaths used to come early in confinement; during the pandemic and opioid crisis they shifted much later, and long stays plus restrictive pandemic rules tracked with higher mortality. Nelson calls for shorter incarceration, drug treatment access, and stronger health safeguards.
plos-pone-0354732:
Rainer Mere and three colleagues published this 2026 scoping review of the theory frameworks behind process evaluations of community mental health programs. Such evaluations explain how programs work, not just whether. Searching three databases, they found eighty-three studies using fifty-four different primary theoretical frameworks, which they sorted into a family tree by outlook and purpose.

Framework use has shifted over two decades from community-engaged approaches toward tidy, systematized ones. Mere warns that the tidy turn may silence community voices, and offers the typology to help evaluators pick suitable frameworks deliberately.
plos-pone-0341532:
Mohan and Biro, in a 2026 experiment, watch how pairs of people invent shared conventions, the unwritten rules a group settles on to coordinate. Their task copies a color-matching game first used with baboons. Partners had to agree, through play, on which color should win when two colors met.

Pairs got different amounts of help: some could see a partner's screen, and some were told how the task worked. More upfront knowledge slowed the birth of a shared rule, rather than speeding it. Pairs kept their rule even when they could see each other's screens and a simpler trick was open to them. When a seasoned player was paired with a newcomer, a rule formed fast, but the newcomer's rule was not a copy of the veteran's. Know-how passed between partners, the authors argue, more readily than the content of the rule itself.
plos-pone-0352932:
Yuxuan He and seven co-authors examine how the burden of anxiety disorders differs between middle-income and high-income countries in this 2026 PLOS ONE analysis. Drawing on a major global health database, they tracked cases, prevalence, and years of healthy life lost from 1990 through 2023. They also projected trends forward to 2035 and weighed the role of violence-related risks.

Anxiety remained heavy and unevenly spread, with clear gaps by income group, sex, and age. Partner violence, bullying, and childhood sexual violence each accounted for part of the harm. The team urges mental health plans shaped to income level and aimed at preventing violence, especially where services are scarce.
plos-pone-0354032:
Xavier Sánchez and four colleagues survey medical trainees in Ecuador about the link between a positive mental attitude and depression, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Seven hundred students and residents at a private university completed a standard depression screening scale and a questionnaire on health habits, covering diet, exercise, rest, and outlook. Nearly half screened positive for significant depressive symptoms.

Of all the habit domains, only positive mental attitude — a hopeful, constructive way of framing events — stayed linked to lower odds of depression once the others were accounted for. Women, younger trainees, and those with other illnesses fared worse. The authors argue medical schools should teach positive-psychology skills, not just clinical ones.
plos-pone-0352032:
Naja and colleagues surveyed young children's eating in the United Arab Emirates in a 2026 study. More than four hundred children aged four to nine were measured and their diets recalled in detail across three emirates. Sorting foods into broad patterns can show habits that single food counts would miss.

Two patterns stood out: a healthy one rich in fruit, vegetables, olive oil, and whole grains, and a Western one heavy in fast food, salty snacks, sweets, and sweet drinks. Children scoring high on the healthy pattern had lower weight-for-age scores. About one in five children was overweight or at risk, which makes the contrast useful for building food programs that fit local culture.
plos-pone-0346532:
Chen and colleagues built a risk score for sepsis from routine blood gas tests in a 2026 study. Sepsis kills many intensive care patients, and existing scores need many inputs. Records came from two large American intensive care databases, one used to build the score and both used to check it.

The score joins three blood gas measures: oxygen, acid balance, and lactate. It predicted death within twenty-eight days on its own, and high-risk patients were clearly sicker. A chart form of the score beat older scales in their tests. Because blood gases are already drawn in every intensive care unit, the score asks for no new tests.
plos-pone-0352332:
Debbie Gach and seven co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One study of long-term health after COVID-19 in the Netherlands. They compared patients who had the post COVID-19 condition, the lingering illness often called long COVID, with patients who did not. More than a year after infection, people from three hospitals took wide-ranging checks. The checks covered quality of life, lungs, body chemistry, strength, thinking, mood, and social life.

Those with the lingering condition felt clearly worse. They reported poorer quality of life, more fatigue, more anxiety, and poorer sleep. They also scored lower on breathing-muscle strength and exercise capacity. Yet most lab and scan tests showed no gap between the groups. Formal thinking tests showed no gap either. The authors stress this mismatch. Patients feel far worse than standard tests can explain, which makes care and recognition harder.
plos-pone-0348432:
Zhonghan Wu and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One surgical study of a curved guide tool nicknamed the Gold Wrist. The tool helps place the guidewire when nailing a broken hip. The patients were obese, with weak bones, which makes the operation risky. Five hundred such patients at one center were split evenly. Half had surgery with the new guide, and half with standard tools.

The guided group had shorter operations and smaller cuts. Their inflammation markers were lower. Their early hip function scores were better. Internal complications, like clots, lung embolism, and infection, were far fewer. Hospital costs were lower too, as was the estimated carbon footprint. Computer modeling confirmed the device is sound. The authors present it as a practical aid for a high-risk operation.
plos-pone-0353032:
Toshiko Mori and six colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study of a urine marker that may catch diabetic kidney disease earlier than standard tests. The usual measures mainly reflect damage to the kidney's filters and can miss early injury to its tubules, including patients whose urine protein looks normal. In more than two hundred Japanese outpatients with type 2 diabetes, the team measured modified fragments of the protein fetuin-A in urine.

Higher levels of the marker were independently tied to worse kidney risk categories, roughly quadrupling the odds of being in a higher-risk group. It was already raised in a substantial share of patients whose standard tests looked reassuring, unlike a comparison tubular marker that only rose late. The authors propose it as a complement to existing tests for earlier risk sorting.
plos-pone-0349232:
Rathi Ravindrarajah and colleagues evaluated a digital self-help service for people with type two diabetes in Greater Manchester during the pandemic. The service, MyWay Diabetes, gives patients online access to their records and learning tools. The team compared about five hundred users with a matched group of non-users over two years of follow-up.

Users showed a clear drop in long-term blood sugar compared with non-users, plus small gains in blood pressure and cholesterol. A long-range model then weighed health gains against costs and found the service good value, possibly even saving money once medicines were counted. The authors say digital support of this kind can help clinics care for more patients between visits.
plos-pone-0351632:
Cynthia Osei and co-authors studied three hundred sixty-five people with high blood pressure at a university hospital in Kumasi, Ghana, tracing how family life affects their health. Taking medicine faithfully is known to improve quality of life, but relatives who remind, cook, pay, and encourage may be part of why. Questionnaires measured adherence, family support, and quality of life for each patient.

Patients who stuck to their medicine reported better quality of life, and family support carried part of that effect: support helped adherence, and adherence helped life feel better. The chain means clinics gain by treating the family as part of the prescription. In settings where relatives already share care work, inviting them into blood pressure management is a cheap lever with real payoff, provided the patient's own wishes lead.
plos-pone-0351832:
Farm soil near mines can quietly gather toxic metals, and Ying Hu and co-authors sampled fields around the Baiyun Mountain mining area in Nanyang, China. Their 2026 PLOS One study tested more than four hundred surface samples for nine metals and elements, including silver, copper, lead, and arsenic.

Zinc, molybdenum, and mercury stood well above the natural background for the province. A risk model rated the overall ecological danger, and a source-fitting model split the pollution among likely origins such as mining, farming, and rock itself. Mapping where each metal concentrates helps local officials decide which fields need watching or cleanup first.
plos-pone-0350732:
Self-driving cars must spot rare dangers: fallen trees, loose barrels, scattered debris. Afeera Bint-e Tanveer and colleagues trained a compact vision model, YOLOv8-n, for exactly these roadside surprises, in this 2026 PLOS One study aimed at cheaper on-board hardware.

Images from several open collections were merged and cleaned into one training set. Extra training images with changed brightness, tilts, and partial blocking taught the model to cope with bad light and clutter. On a mid-range graphics card it read sixty-eight images per second with high precision and recall. The authors say such lean models suit cars that cannot carry data-center hardware.
plos-pone-0349632:
How happy citizens feel with public services varies sharply across Peru's coast, mountains, and jungle. Miluska Odely Rodriguez-Saavedra and colleagues analyzed a 2024 national household survey covering nearly thirty-four thousand people and twenty-one public services, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Scores differed significantly across the eight geographic domains, though the overall gap was modest in size. City and countryside answers diverged as well. A statistical grouping step explored whether services cluster into a few underlying dimensions of satisfaction. The authors say national averages hide regional discontent, and improvement plans should be drawn region by region rather than from Lima alone.
plos-pone-0351132:
South China Sea knowledge lies scattered across many sources. Historical, legal, and political texts span centuries. Ruinan Zhao, Zhifan Han, and Huiling Liu used a large language model to join them. They built a knowledge graph from the sources. A knowledge graph stores facts as linked triples. Computers can search and reason over it.

The pipeline works in three stages. It extracts facts, standardizes names, and verifies links. The finished graph holds nearly sixty thousand entities. It stores over six hundred fifty thousand fact triples. Users can answer questions across eras. Hidden multi-step connections also surface. The authors offer the method for other tangled domains.
plos-pone-0349732:
Agnes Karingo Karume and colleagues describe a trial plan, with no results yet, for adding mental health care into routine pregnancy clinics in Kenya. Low mood and anxiety around birth are common, yet trained specialists are scarce. Twenty clinics in western Kenya will be split by chance into two arms. Close to three thousand pregnant women will take part.

Clinics in the main arm will screen every woman, offer talk support from trained lay helpers for mild to moderate cases, and use video psychiatry for severe cases or poor response. Other clinics will screen and refer as usual. The team will compare health gains, service reach, and how well the model fits daily clinic work.
plos-pone-0350932:
Yuxing Wang and colleagues stretched frozen loess, a wind blown soil, to test how added plastic fibres change its strength in the cold. Frozen ground strength guides building in cold regions and frost heave forecasts. Custom gear pulled samples with varied fibre doses, freezing levels, and pull speeds, while microscopes revealed the soil inner structure.

Fibres turned clean breaks into slow, cracked stretching and raised load capacity greatly. A dose near three tenths of one percent worked best, lifting strength by over seventy percent. Colder samples grew stronger fast, and faster pulling also raised strength. Too many fibres clumped and weakened the soil. A light fibre dose, properly mixed, toughens frozen ground for foundations and slopes.
plos-pone-0351232:
Christiane Al-Haddad and colleagues used a scan that maps tiny eye blood vessels to compare children with lazy eye, their fellow eye, and healthy controls. Lazy eye, or amblyopia, affects vision in one eye in childhood. Seventy eight children took part, half with lazy eye split evenly between crossing and focus mismatch causes, with average age near ten.

Lazy eyes showed higher vessel and flow density in outer and full centre zones than control eyes. The dark centre spot with no vessels was smaller in lazy eyes than in fellow eyes. Disc measures mostly matched controls. Vessel growth may overcompensate in lazy eyes, a clue that the condition reaches beyond the brain visual centres.
plos-pone-0350232:
Katarzyna Hildt-Ciupinska, Karolina Pawlowska-Cyprysiak, and Zofia Mockallo surveyed nine hundred and twenty seven working women in Poland, aged eighteen to sixty five, on health habits, well being, and work ability. Online forms used standard well being and work ability indexes plus a positive health behaviour scale scored out of one hundred and two points.

Average behaviour scores sat in the middle, near sixty points. Health care effort rose with age, and office workers scored above physical and mixed workers. Better health habits linked clearly with higher well being and stronger work ability. Workplace health teaching, the authors argue, is a practical lever employers control directly.
plos-pone-0328432:
Sergio Delle Monache and a team in Italy studied how the eye follows a falling object that briefly vanishes, in 2026 work. Catching relies on the brain predicting motion under gravity, and the team asked whether doing a hand task at the same time changes that prediction.

Volunteers tracked targets that fell truly or with altered gravity, against plain or realistic scenes, while some also reached to intercept. Eye movements showed a blend of fresh visual input and gravity based prediction, and the mix shifted with task and scene. The results help explain how people time catches when sight is briefly blocked.
plos-pone-0349932:
Ismaila Ajayi Yusuf and co-authors pooled trials of a new class of blood pressure drugs in 2026. The drugs block the making of aldosterone, a hormone that raises pressure, and no trial had yet pitched them against each other directly.

Seven randomised trials with nearly three thousand patients were combined in a network analysis. All the drugs lowered systolic pressure clearly against dummy pills, with one agent showing the largest drop. Effects differed between hard to control and truly resistant cases. The ranking gives doctors an early map of a promising class, while head to head trials are still missing.
plos-pone-0350132:
Haiming Liang and co-authors searched for uric acid related genes in diabetic retinopathy in 2026. The eye disease is a leading cause of blindness in diabetes, and uric acid, the gout chemical, seems to play a part in its course.

Public gene data were screened by several methods, and two candidate genes stood out with higher levels in patient blood samples. Pathway checks tied them to distinct signalling and protein handling routes. Immune cell patterns in the samples also shifted, and the genes related in opposite ways to natural killer cells. Two genes will not explain a complex disease, but they offer testable leads for early detection.
plos-pone-0350332:
Amlak Abaza and co-authors modelled solid oxide fuel cells in 2026, using a nature inspired search method to fit the model's unknown values. These fuel cells convert fuel to power cleanly for vehicles and buildings, but accurate models need careful tuning.

The search method, modelled on predator and prey behaviour, was paired with a switching strategy that changes tactics by phase. The stack model was tested at four temperatures, with some runs kept for validation. Against several known methods the new pairing fit experimental curves closely. Better fitting matters because engineers design and control real stacks from these models, not from prototypes alone.
plos-pone-0346732:
Kanokphol Supasirimontri, Vilai Kuptniratsaikul, and Metita Wiwitkul tested five fast screens for muscle loss. The patients were older adults in stroke rehab wards. The state is called sarcopenia: low muscle mass plus weak grip. Missing it slows recovery. Full tests take time and gear. The team checked all five screens on one hundred fourteen patients in 2026.

Half the patients had the condition. A tape measure around the calf worked best. Cutoffs sat just above thirty centimeters, with a slightly lower mark for women. A short survey plus the tape also did well. The three survey-only tools were much weaker. The team backs the tape as the ward's first screen.
plos-pone-0350032:
Kristina M Kokorelias and Annie Robitaille published a 2026 protocol for mapping what helps and hinders putting childcare services inside long-term care homes. Such homes struggle to hire and keep staff, many of whom juggle young children, and on-site childcare could steady the workforce while giving residents time with children. No synthesis of the implementation evidence existed.

As a protocol, the document lays out the planned review: searches across five databases plus grey literature, duplicate screening, and a thematic sorting of barriers and supports using an established implementation framework. Care home and childcare staff will help interpret the findings. The authors expect the map to expose evidence gaps and guide homes considering the model.
plos-pone-0349132:
Yuping Yan and colleagues propose an algorithm that adjusts how often electrical substation equipment gets serviced, based on the equipment's actual condition rather than a fixed calendar. Substations keep power grids stable, and servicing too late risks failures while servicing too early wastes money. Sensors across the substation feed live condition data into their system.

The method weighs the cost of planned maintenance against the cost of a failure, then solves for the service interval that balances the two. Scheduling limits, such as how daily plans and start times interact, act as constraints. The result is a maintenance cycle that shifts as equipment ages or weakens, a step toward smarter grid upkeep.
plos-pone-0349432:
Jie Guo, Renjing Liu, and Jinsheng Xing address two headaches in federated learning, where many devices train a shared model without handing over their data. Sending model updates back and forth eats bandwidth, and ordinary encryption can fail when several parties collude. Their scheme trims unneeded parts of the model automatically, guided by accuracy feedback, and encrypts updates with several keys at once.

With multiple keys, the central server can combine encrypted updates without ever decrypting them, and the design resists collusion by nearly all parties. Tests on two standard image datasets showed the trimming sharply cut both local computing and the volume sent each round. The authors aim the approach at phones and edge devices with little spare power or bandwidth.
plos-pone-0349032:
Youngju Lee and colleagues scanned the brains of forty shoppers deciding whether to buy shoes, to find out why free shipping feels so good. The total price never changed; only the split between the shoe price and the delivery fee moved. Participants rated their wish to buy while a scanner watched which brain areas woke up for each price arrangement.

Free shipping won clearly, and the brain showed why: choosing it lit up a region tied to positive emotion, especially when compared against even the smallest fee. It was as if zero delivery carries a special emotional charge beyond saving money. As fees grew, that emotional glow faded and cooler calculating regions took over. The authors say sellers are not imagining it; the pull of free shipping is wired into how the deciding brain responds.
plos-pone-0347932:
Patricia Orlandi Barth and co-workers evaluate a home-built machine reader that measures antibiotic test discs in a working microbiology lab. Such tests show which drugs still kill a patient's germs, and reading the clear zones by ruler is slow and varies by reader. Their 2026 study compares the reader with manual measures across five hundred tests and thousands of zones.

The two methods agreed on the drug call in nearly ninety-seven of a hundred cases. Serious errors were rare, and zone sizes tracked each other closely. Automating this reading could standardize results between staff and speed up answers for doctors choosing antibiotics. The trial shows a locally built tool can hold its own in daily lab work.
plos-pone-0346432:
Remya Ampadi Ramachandran and co-workers train machine learning models to predict how fast animals clear a drug from the body, a key number for setting doses. Direct clearance data are missing for many drug and species pairs. Their 2026 study mines published studies for drug, dose, species, and route details, then races nine models on the assembled data in several slices.

Simple regression, a small neural network, and a forest model led the pack overall. Accuracy jumped higher still when models focused on single animal groups such as hoofed stock or pets. Separate handling of skewed data through resampling kept rare cases from being swamped. Veterinarians and researchers could estimate dosing gaps before running costly animal studies.
plos-pone-0348632:
Qiyue Song and three co-workers asked what makes fans of metaverse music apps post their own work. These apps mix songs with virtual worlds you can roam. The survey reached four hundred thirty-five users in China. It split the pull of the apps into two paths: a social path and a lost-in-the-moment path.

Warmth and the sense of real people near by fed the social path. Dressing an avatar, tales, and rich sights and sounds fed the flow path. Both paths made the apps feel more dear, and that dear feel drove posting. Trust in the tech boosted just the social path. App makers can use that split.
plos-pone-0348232:
Aryalakshmi Sreemohan and colleagues examined nearly fifteen hundred hospitalised dengue patients at an Indian tertiary centre between 2021 and 2024, asking who dies and how the liver shapes the odds. Dengue attacks the liver in most admitted patients. The team graded liver involvement, hunted for death predictors, and checked whether existing prognostic scores work in this infection.

About five percent died. Severe dengue, intensive care admission, a high inflammation ratio, and above all low blood albumin predicted death. Surprisingly, patients with fatty liver survived better than those with healthy livers, while decompensated cirrhosis fared worst. A simple albumin-based grade separated risk well. Machine grouping found four patient types with very different death rates.
plos-pone-0348132:
Parviz Shahmirzalou and Hassan Ebrahimpour Sadagheyani read three years of bite logs in Khoy County, Iran. Bites count there chiefly through rabies, a near sure death once signs start. The logs span from the spring of 2021 to the spring of 2024. The team asked who gets bit, by what beast, and in which months.

Rates ran high each year, at times near five hundred per lakh of folk. Dogs made nine in ten bites, most in sudden strikes. Warm months saw the most bites. The team's forecast sees the same peak next year. They urge more teaching for at-risk groups and fast shots post-bite.
plos-pone-0347032:
Baochen Su and colleagues surveyed nearly two thousand Chinese university students confined to campus during COVID-19 closures, asking what protected their quality of life. Mental component scores sagged well below physical ones. Their 2026 analysis weighed psychological distress, daily habits, and career planning against standard health-related quality of life measures.

Low distress was the strongest shield for both body and mind scores. Regular exercise and a steady study routine helped substantially, and students with clear career plans fared better physically and mentally. Having a romantic partner, oddly, cut both ways. The authors urge universities in future crises to bundle mental health support, lifestyle guidance, and career services together.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
A claim of invasion in Laos sent a Council fact team to Asia in 1959. On 7 September, it adopted Resolution 132. Ten members voted yes and one voted no. The Soviet Union was the lone no. Laos, neutral under the 1954 Geneva deal, charged that North Vietnamese troops fought on its soil. The Council heard claims it could not check from New York.

The text names a four-member sub-panel to look into it. Argentina, Italy, Japan, and Tunisia hold the seats. The panel must study the claims made before the Council. It may take fresh statements and papers as well. Any inquiries it finds needful are in its remit. Its report is due as soon as can be. No clear proof of invasion came back from the trip.

Angola's long civil war had just ended when Resolution 1432 passed unanimously on 15 August 2002. The government and the UNITA rebels had signed a ceasefire addendum on 4 April 2002. UNITA soldiers were being demobilized. On 2 August the movement disbanded its military wing. It was turning toward politics.

To help the peace hold, the Council suspended some sanctions on UNITA. The travel bans dated from 1997. They were lifted for another ninety days under Chapter VII. Free movement would let UNITA members join the peace process. It would also aid national reconciliation. Members said they might review the measures before the ninety days ran out.

Kazakhstan was the largest republic to leave the Soviet Union in land terms. Its independence came in December 1991. An application for UN membership followed quickly. Resolution 732, adopted without a vote on 23 January 1992, took up the request at the Council's 3034th meeting.

Members advised the General Assembly to admit the Republic of Kazakhstan. The Assembly acted in March 1992. The new state inherited Soviet nuclear weapons on its soil. That fact gave its arrival unusual weight in security debates. Kazakhstan later gave those weapons up. Its admission formed part of the broad post-Soviet intake that reshaped the UN in early 1992.

Israeli commandos raided Beirut in April 1973, killing Palestinian leaders. Lebanon brought its outrage to the Council. Members grieved the civilian deaths caused by cross-border violence. Resolution 332 was adopted on 21 April 1973. Eleven members voted yes. China, Guinea, the Soviet Union, and the United States abstained.

The Council condemned every act of violence that harms innocent people. It then condemned Israel's repeated military attacks on Lebanon by name. Those attacks broke the Charter, the 1949 armistice, and past ceasefire orders. Israel was told to stop all such attacks at once. The text balances two angers: at raids on Lebanon, and at the wider cycle of killings endangering civilians and air travel.

Resolution 1032, adopted unanimously on 19 December 1995, keeps the UN force in Cyprus into 1996. The Secretary-General's December report had recommended extending UNFICYP, and Cyprus agreed the force was still needed beyond the year's end. The Council noted with concern that no progress had been made toward a final political settlement, nor on widening a 1989 agreement to unman sensitive posts along the buffer zone.

The mandate was extended to 30 June 1996. Military authorities on both sides were told to prevent incidents along the buffer zone and cooperate fully with the force. The Secretary-General was asked to review the force's structure and strength with an eye to restructuring it.

Walvis Bay belongs to Namibia, Resolution 432 declares; it was adopted unanimously on 28 July 1978. Walvis Bay was a deep-water port enclave on Namibia's coast that South Africa administered as its own, separate from the territory around it. The General Assembly had already called the port an integral part of Namibia in 1977.

The Council declared that Namibia's territorial integrity and unity must be secured by bringing Walvis Bay back within its territory. It promised full support for steps toward that early reintegration. Until it happened, South Africa was told not to use the bay in any way that harmed Namibia's independence or economic viability. The port was in fact handed over in 1994, four years after independence.

Resolution 1832, adopted on 27 August 2008, extends the UN force in southern Lebanon for another year, unchanged. Lebanon's prime minister had written on 18 August asking for a one-year renewal without amendment, and the Secretary-General recommended granting it. The Council praised UNIFIL's active role and the dedication of its personnel and commander since the force was strengthened after the 2006 war.

The present mandate was extended until 31 August 2009. The Council restated its commitment to carrying out resolution 1701 in full, the text that ended the 2006 fighting and promised a permanent ceasefire and long-term settlement. It also underlined that UNIFIL must have every means and piece of equipment its mandate requires.

Sierra Leone's military junta is sanctioned in Resolution 1132, adopted on 8 October 1997. The junta that seized power on 25 May 1997 had refused to restore the democratically elected government, violence and humanitarian conditions were worsening, and ECOWAS had agreed sanctions at Abuja.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands the junta relinquish power immediately and make way for constitutional order. It imposes a travel ban on junta members and adult family members, as designated by a new sanctions Committee, and an embargo on petroleum products and arms to Sierra Leone. The Committee may authorize exceptions case by case, including petroleum imports for the elected government and for humanitarian or ECOMOG needs. Acting also under Chapter VIII, the Council authorizes ECOWAS to enforce the embargo, including by halting inward shipping to inspect and verify cargoes, and requires thirty-day ECOWAS reports. The measures end when the junta complies.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 32, adopted on 9 February 1946 at the twenty-sixth plenary meeting, dealt with Spain and its standing at the new United Nations. The Assembly recalled the San Francisco ruling. Under it, the Charter's membership terms could not fit states whose regimes had been set up with help from the armed forces of countries that fought the United Nations. That held while those regimes lasted.

The text also recalled the Potsdam statement that the leading Allied governments would not back membership for the sitting Spanish government, founded with Axis support. The Assembly backed both statements and urged members to guide their dealings with Spain by their letter and spirit.

Resolution 69/32 of the General Assembly, 'No first placement of weapons in outer space,' urges an early start to work on a treaty banning weapons in orbit. It welcomes the draft treaty against placing weapons in outer space or using force against space objects. The draft was tabled by China and the Russian Federation at the Conference on Disarmament in 2008. It was updated in 2014. Pending a treaty, the Assembly encourages all states, especially space-faring nations, to pledge not to be the first to place weapons in space.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Congo's peacekeeping mission, MONUC, is kept in place by this text of 14 December 2000. The Lusaka Ceasefire Agreement was still largely unimplemented and fighting went on. At the same time, new deals on pulling forces apart had just been reached at Maputo and Harare, and the Council wanted observers ready to check them.

MONUC's mandate now ran to 15 June 2001, and the Council backed sending more military observers once conditions allowed. Those observers would verify that the parties kept the ceasefire and carried out the agreed pullbacks. All parties were called on to stop fighting, honour the chain of peace deals, and cooperate fully with the mission.

Liberia's former president and his circle have their wealth frozen in this text of 12 March 2004. The Council found that Charles Taylor and his associates had drained Liberia's resources and hidden funds and property abroad. From exile, he still controlled much of that money and could use it to stir up trouble in Liberia and the region.

Acting under Chapter VII, all states are ordered to freeze funds and assets owned or controlled by Taylor. The freeze also covers his immediate family, senior officials of his former regime, and close allies named by the sanctions committee. The freeze is meant to keep that money from wrecking Liberia's recovery, with the aim that the assets eventually be returned for the benefit of its people.

The Group of Experts watching the arms embargo on Côte d'Ivoire is extended until 15 December 2005 in this text of 18 October 2005. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council noted that the situation in the country still threatened peace in the region. The group was asked to send a brief written update through the sanctions committee before its term ended, ahead of a fuller report.

Its own sanctions working group is closed down on 21 December 2006. The Informal Working Group on General Issues of Sanctions had been asked to develop general recommendations for making United Nations sanctions work better. The Council decided the group had fulfilled that mandate. It took note with interest of the best practices and methods in the group's report and asked its own subsidiary bodies to take note of them as well.

The war crimes court for Rwanda faced a familiar problem in June 2010: it could not finish its work on time. Resolution 1932, adopted on 29 June 2010, deals with that court, which was set up after the genocide of 1994. Its president warned that experienced staff were leaving before the trials ended.

The Council extended the terms of the court's appeals judges until the end of 2012. Trial judges, both permanent and temporary, would serve until the end of 2011, or until their cases finished. The court could also bring back a former judge as a temporary judge if no judge on its roster was free. States were pressed to help arrest the fugitives who were still at large. The point was to let the last trials finish properly.

A year of appeals had failed to end the rebellion in Southern Rhodesia. On 16 December 1966 the Council adopted Resolution 232, which turned the pressure into binding sanctions. The white minority regime still held power after its one-sided declaration of independence from Britain. British measures had not brought the rebellion to an end.

The Council ruled that the situation was a threat to international peace and security. All member states had to block imports of key Rhodesian goods. The list included asbestos, iron ore, chrome, sugar, tobacco, copper, meat, and hides. Arms, aircraft, and vehicles had to be kept from the regime. States were also told to give the illegal government no financial or economic aid. These were the first binding sanctions of this kind in United Nations history.

Fighting continued in Indonesia in the summer of 1947 between Dutch forces and the Republic of Indonesia. Resolution 32, adopted on 26 August 1947, is a short reminder to both sides. It recalls Resolution 27 of that year, with its cease-fire order and call for a peaceful settlement. The Netherlands and the Republic of Indonesia were called on to stick strictly to the Council's recommendation of 1 August 1947. Nothing new was added; the point was to hold both governments to the earlier order.
un-sc-res-132: Claims about foreign troops inside Laos reached the Council in 1959. On 7 September 1959 it set up a sub-committee to look into them. Argentina, Italy, Japan, and Tunisia supplied the members. The group had to study the statements made before the Council. It could gather more statements and papers. It could also run inquiries of its own. A report was due as soon as possible. The vote was ten to one, with the Soviet Union against. The step let the Council test the claims without yet judging them.
un-sc-res-1432:
Angola's peace held through the summer of 2002, and sanctions stayed paused. On 15 August 2002 the Security Council added ninety days to a suspension of measures on UNITA. The limits came from resolution 1127 of 1997. They had first been paused that May. The April memorandum between the government and UNITA had ended the fighting. The Council wanted to encourage the peace process further.

Before the new period ended, the Council could review the measures again. It would weigh all facts, including word from Angola's government. The review would test how well the peace accords were being used. Suspension was a reward with a clock on it. Full lifting of the sanctions came later that year.
un-sc-res-332:
An Israeli raid on Beirut in April 1973 brought Lebanon's protest to the Council. On 21 April 1973 the Council voiced deep concern at all acts of violence. It grieved the loss of innocent life in the recent attacks. Lebanon and Israel had both spoken. Truce records showed a pattern of broken resolutions. The Council's anger in the text runs in both directions, but its formal blame lands on one side.

The Council condemns Israel's repeated military attacks on Lebanon. Those attacks broke Lebanon's sovereignty and the Charter. They also broke the armistice deal between the two states. Israel had to stop all such attacks at once. The warning closed a tense debate on cross-border raids.
un-sc-res-1032:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was renewed by the Security Council on 19 December 1995. The Secretary-General's report of 10 December advised keeping the United Nations Peace-keeping Force in Cyprus. The island's government agreed it should stay past 31 December 1995. No progress had been made toward a final political solution, the Council noted with concern.

The Council extended UNFICYP's mandate to 30 June 1996. Military authorities on both sides were told to keep the buffer zone free of incidents and to cooperate fully with the force. The Secretary-General was asked to keep the force's structure and size under review for possible change. The Council backed the force's advice on living conditions for Greek Cypriots and Maronites in the north and Turkish Cypriots in the south. It also voiced concern at growing military spending and the failure to extend the 1989 unmanning deal along the whole buffer zone.
un-sc-res-432:
Walvis Bay's place inside Namibia was declared by the Security Council in July 1978. The Council recalled resolution 385 (1976) and its own resolution 431 (1978), adopted the same day as this text. The General Assembly had declared in November 1977 that Walvis Bay is an integral part of Namibia. South Africa held the port enclave apart from the rest of the territory it occupied.

The Council declared that Namibia's territorial integrity and unity must be assured by bringing Walvis Bay back within its territory. It promised full support for the steps needed to win the port's early return. Until that day, South Africa must not use Walvis Bay in any way that harmed Namibia's independence or the health of its economy. The Council stayed seized of the matter until the bay was fully reintegrated. The port stayed in South African hands until 1994.
un-sc-res-1832:
UNIFIL's mandate was extended for a further year on 27 August 2008. Lebanon's prime minister had written on 18 August asking for one more year without change. The Secretary-General advised the same on 21 August. The Council praised the force and its commander, and it restated its pledge to carry out resolution 1701 (2006) in full. Lebanon's state of affairs still threatened regional peace, it found.

The Council extended UNIFIL's present mandate until 31 August 2009. It praised the force's positive role. Its deployment beside the Lebanese Armed Forces had built a new strategic setting in the south, the Council said. Joint work between the force and the Lebanese army was welcomed and urged to grow. All parties were called to respect the halt to hostilities and the Blue Line along its whole length. They also had to work fully with the United Nations and guard UNIFIL staff.
un-sc-res-1132:
The Security Council turned to Sierra Leone in Resolution 1132, adopted on 8 October 1997. A military junta had seized power in a coup on 25 May 1997. It refused to step aside for the elected government. Violence spread, aid was blocked, and hunger deepened across the country.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands that the junta give up power at once. It bans the sale of oil, fuel, and arms to Sierra Leone. Junta members and their adult families face a travel ban. West African states may stop ships at sea to enforce the bans. A sanctions committee will track compliance and grant narrow aid exceptions. The bans end when the elected government returns.
un-un-res-sixth-report-of-the-secretary-:
Late 2000 in Sierra Leone is covered by the sixth report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Mission there, document S/2000/832. UNAMSIL had survived its spring hostage crisis and was being rebuilt with more troops and a firmer mandate. A fresh ceasefire was being tested on the ground.

The report describes patrols, disarmament steps, and the slow return of state control to rebel-held areas. It also deals with the diamond trade that funded the war. The text shows a mission moving, with care, from survival toward real peace work.
europmc-pmc10016932:
Umakanthan and colleagues review what was known about COVID-19 in a 2020 paper, covering its origin, spread, diagnosis, and care. Coronaviruses had already caused two major outbreaks in two decades. The new disease, first seen in late 2019, was spreading across the world as they wrote.

The authors explain where the virus likely came from and how it passes between people. They survey the tests used to confirm infection and the care given to patients. The paper stands as a compact record of early knowledge, written while the pandemic was still young.
europmc-pmc10183032:
Zhao and colleagues review the role of gut microbes in cancer therapy in a 2023 paper, from molecular mechanisms to clinical use. Fast DNA sequencing has revealed how deeply the gut's microbial community affects cancer growth and treatment response. Patients with similar tumors can respond very differently to the same drug, and gut microbes seem to be one reason.

The review explains how microbes shape immunity and drug metabolism. It gathers evidence on diet, probiotics, and stool transfer as ways to aid therapy. It also notes the care needed, since cancer patients are fragile.
europmc-pmc10451032:
Hu and co-authors tested in 2023 how changes in a virus enzyme could defeat a key Covid drug. The drug, nirmatrelvir, blocks the main protease of SARS-CoV-2, a tool the virus uses to build itself. New variants raised fears that the drug might fail. The team built and checked 102 changed forms of the enzyme.

Twenty-two changes at five spots kept the enzyme strong yet shrugged off the drug. Hu mapped the shapes of six of these forms with X-ray methods. Live virus tests then proved the resistance in full virus. Some drug-proof forms grew more weakly, a small comfort. The team flags these spots for close watch in clinics.
europmc-pmc10564932:
Huangfu and co-authors reviewed the IL-17 family of immune signals in 2023. The family holds six members, named IL-17A through IL-17F. Their matching receptors have all been found in recent years. These signals stir swelling during infection and immune disease. They also help the body fight germs.

That dual role makes the family hard to pin down. Huangfu traces the signal chain each member sets off in cells. The chain guards tissue, drives repair, and can feed cancer growth. Two disease cases get close study: lupus, an immune attack on the body, and spread of tumours. The review closes with drug and test gains for immune disease and cancer.
europmc-pmc10687432:
Basak and co-authors reviewed tumour-linked macrophages in 2023 and why immune therapy often fails. Macrophages form the bulk of immune cells inside a tumour. They come in two broad kinds: M1, which fights cancer, and M2, which shields it. Tumours tilt the mix toward M2 to secure their growth.

That tilt speeds blood vessel growth, spread, and immune shutdown, Basak reports. It also helps seed cancer stem cells, which can restart a tumour after care. The stem cells return the favour with escape tricks of their own. Weak grasp of this crosstalk helps explain stalled immune drugs. The review backs plans that strike cancer cells, stem cells, and macrophages at once.
europmc-pmc10873332:
Quintard and a large team built a chip system that grows tiny organs with working blood vessels in this 2024 paper. Organoids are small 3D cell clusters that mimic organs in the lab. They need blood vessels to survive long term, yet adding vessels on chips has stayed hard. Most devices also fail to copy the flow patterns found in the body.

Their platform grew vessel networks around cell balls and vessel organoids for up to 30 days. The networks linked up and carried flow into the tissues, the team reports. Tissues on the chip grew, matured, and worked better than those grown without flow. The system was tested on support cells and insulin-making cell clusters. The authors present it as a base for more lifelike organ models in drug testing.
europmc-pmc11093732:
Pachitariu, Sridhar, Pennington, and Stringer present a new version of a brain signal sorting tool in this 2024 paper. Electrodes in the brain record mixed electrical spikes from many nerve cells at once. Spike sorting is the computing task of assigning each spike to one cell. It is hard because recordings drift and the fields of nearby cells overlap.

Their tool, Kilosort4, adds clustering methods inspired by graph maths, the study of linked networks. To test it fairly, they built simulations from densely sampled real recordings with realistic noise and drift. Kilosort4 beat rival tools in all tested conditions, they report. It correctly found even faint cells and tiny cells under heavy drift. Earlier versions also beat most rivals. The framework is developed openly for the field to use.
europmc-pmc11126432:
Jeblick and colleagues test whether ChatGPT can rewrite radiology reports in plain words in this 2024 case study. Radiology reports are written for doctors, and patients often cannot parse them. Large language models, AI systems trained on vast text, might simplify them. The team asked whether the simplified versions stay correct and safe.

A radiologist wrote three fictitious reports, and ChatGPT rewrote each for a child, as prompted. Fifteen radiologists then rated the rewrites for correctness, completeness, and risk of harm. Most raters judged the rewrites correct, complete, and not harmful. Still, raters flagged some wrong statements, missed facts, and risky passages. The authors see large potential for patient-centred care. They also stress that the tool needs further adaptation to medicine before routine use.
europmc-pmc11461632:
Hu and colleagues review how metabolism regulates the immune system in health and disease in this 2024 paper. Immune cells run on metabolic pathways such as glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation, and fatty acid oxidation, meaning burning sugar, burning fuel with oxygen, and burning fat. Which pathway dominates shapes what an immune cell does. The concept linking the two fields is called immunometabolism.

Introduced over a decade ago, the concept has widened from chronic low-grade inflammation to metabolic reprogramming across diseases. In cancer, autoimmune disease, and metabolic disease, reprogrammed immune cells turn pro-inflammatory or anti-inflammatory. Those shifts then drive disease development, the authors trace. The review summarises the mechanisms pathway by pathway. It closes with interventions that target immune metabolism, from diet-level measures to drugs under study.
europmc-pmc11485232:
Vorontsov and a large team present the largest AI foundation model for pathology to date in this 2024 paper. Foundation models are large AI systems trained on broad data and then adapted to tasks. Pathology AI aims to support clinical decisions and precision medicine, but it must model very diverse tissue patterns. Their model is called Virchow.

Virchow enabled pan-cancer detection across nine common and seven rare cancers, the authors report. Detection reached a specimen-level score of 0.95 on the standard curve measure. Built on Virchow, a detector trained with less labelled data matched clinical-grade tissue-specific models already in production. On some rare cancer variants it outperformed them. The authors also evaluate biomarker prediction and cell identification. They argue the gains show the value of scale where labelled data are scarce.
europmc-pmc11486532:
Ru, Li, Chen, Wu, Min, and Wang review iron balance and iron-driven cell death in human disease in this 2024 paper. Iron is an essential mineral used across body processes, and keeping its levels steady is crucial. Both overload and deficiency cause disorders. Ferroptosis is a cell death that depends on iron and features extensive peroxidation of membrane lipids.

Unlike classic unprogrammed deaths, ferroptosis is tied to disrupted iron metabolism, lipid peroxidation, and antioxidant imbalance, the authors explain. It is regulated at the levels of transcription, translation, and protein modification. Over the past decade it has been linked to cancers, metabolic and autoimmune diseases, brain diseases, heart diseases, and muscle diseases. Ferroptosis proteins are attractive drug targets for incurable diseases. Some such regulators showed benefit in clinical trials.
europmc-pmc1240132:
Blount and co-authors measured plastic chemical traces in urine in 2000. Phthalates are chemicals used widely in plastics and goods. Their breakdown products appear in urine after exposure. Animal work links some of them to reproductive harm.

A new selective method measured seven breakdown products directly. Samples came from 289 adults as a reference group. Three products showed the highest levels overall. Women of childbearing age had higher levels of one key product. Blount gives baseline values for judging exposure in the wider public. It appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2000.
europmc-pmc1280332:
Sioutas, Delfino, and Singh tackled exposure measurement for ultrafine particles in 2005. Health studies had used particle mass as the exposure yardstick. Ultrafine particles behave very differently from larger ones. Their counts and surface area run orders of magnitude higher per mass.

They also carry more oxidant gases, organics, and metals per unit mass. Lab tests show far higher redox activity than larger particles. That chemistry supports a distinct health role. Exposure science for ultrafines is complex, the authors warn. Studies must measure number and surface, not mass alone. A companion paper covers the health evidence in depth.
europmc-pmc1483832:
Two pools of water sat side by side in a Minnesota mine, yet held unlike microbe worlds. Edwards and co-authors read their DNA in 2006 using pyrosequencing, a fast and cheap gene reading method. The two spots in the Soudan Mine differed in chemistry and water flow.

Gene reads showed the microbes ran distinct chemistry on what each pool offered. Paths for carbon use, iron capture, nitrogen uptake, and breathing set the two groups apart. Both groups also differed wholly from any microbe set read before. Edwards argues the method will speed the study of microbe life in the wild.
europmc-pmc1637132:
New neurons born in the adult brain may end up just like those born in youth. Laplagne and co-authors tested that in 2006 in the mouse hippocampus, a region that keeps making neurons for life. They labeled neurons born at each stage with different glow tags.

Recordings from neighbor neurons of different ages showed near-identical wiring. Both received the same balance of excitatory input from the cortex and inhibitory input from local cells. Adult-born neurons fired action potentials like development-born ones. Laplagne proposes the two cohorts form one homogeneous population, a key premise for understanding adult neurogenesis.
europmc-pmc1865532: Late-acting dominant lethal genetic systems and mosquito control. — a 2005 science paper on killer-gene mosquito control. It designs the lethal systems. The paper is the killer-gene study: the findings on mosquito control, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc1950232: Stress and memory: behavioral effects and neurobiological mechanisms. — a 2005 science paper on stress and memory. It reviews the memory effects. The paper is the stress-memory review: the findings on behavioral ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc1961632: Prevention of LPS-induced acute lung injury in mice by mesenchymal stem cells overexpressing angiopoietin 1. — a 2005 science paper on stem cells for lung injury. It prevents the lung injury. The paper is the lung-rescue study: the findings on LPS ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2242832: A mouse model for Chikungunya: young age and inefficient type-I interferon signaling are risk factors for severe disease. — a 2005 science paper on a chikungunya mouse model. It finds the risk factors. The paper is the model study: the findings on chikungunya, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2292732: Meta-analysis of randomized trials: evaluation of benefit from gemcitabine-based combination chemotherapy applied in advanced pancreatic cancer. — a 2005 science paper on gemcitabine mix trials. It grades the mix benefit for labs. The paper is the mix-grade study: the notes on pancreas ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2573032: Estimation of significance thresholds for genomewide association scans. — a 2008 science paper on cutoff lines for gene hunts. It sets the cutoff lines for labs. The paper is the cutoff study: the notes on gene ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2603332: Transmission of influenza virus in a mammalian host is increased by PB2 amino acids 627K or 627 — a 2008 science paper on flu transmission boosters. It finds the PB2 boosters. The paper is the booster study: the findings on influenza, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2606032: A survey of honey bee colony losses in the U.S., fall 2007 to spring 2008. — a 2008 science paper on honey-bee colony losses. It surveys the colony losses. The paper is the survey study: the findings on bee ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2639432: Highly sensitive feature detection for high resolution LC/MS. — a 2008 science paper on LC/MS feature detection. It detects the sensitive features. The paper is the feature study: the findings on LC/MS ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2667632: High levels of exosomes expressing CD63 and caveolin-1 in plasma of melanoma patients. — a 2008 science paper on exosomes in melanoma. It finds the high exosome levels. The paper is the exosome study: the findings on melanoma ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2673032: Implication of the mosquito midgut microbiota in the defense against malaria parasites. — a 2008 science paper on belly germs vs malaria. It links the belly germs for labs. The paper is the belly-germ study: the notes on malaria ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2683932: Significant reduction of antibiotic use in the community after a nationwide campaign in France, — a 2008 science paper on France's antibiotic campaign. It reduces the antibiotic use. The paper is the reduction study: the findings on antibiotic ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2688132: Characteristics and outcomes of cancer patients in European ICUs. — a 2008 science paper on European ICU cancer patients. It lists the patient outcomes. The paper is the outcome study: the findings on cancer ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2700132: Extending an evidence hierarchy to include topics other than treatment: revising the Australian — a 2008 science paper on evidence hierarchies. It extends the evidence hierarchy. The paper is the hierarchy study: the findings on evidence ills, filed here in session.
cory-ancient-fragments-1832:
Isaac Preston Cory gathered surviving fragments of lost pagan writers into one English volume in 1832. Phoenician, Chaldean, Egyptian, Persian, and other traditions all appear in his collection. It was the first English sourcebook of its kind.

Readers met the Chaldean Oracles and Orphic fragments in English here. Cory translated scraps preserved inside later Greek and Latin authors. Nineteenth-century occultists devoured the volume and quoted it for decades. His pioneering collection channeled ancient fragments into the modern imagination. Some translations have aged, and later editions improved many texts. As the doorway through which these fragments reached English readers, it matters.
plos-pone-0004932:
Ewing tumors are cancers of bone and soft tissue. They strike mostly young people. A fused protein called EWS-FLI1 drives them. It forms when two genes wrongly join. Noëlle Guillon and colleagues reported a genome-wide search in PLOS ONE in 2009. They mapped where this fusion protein binds in living tumor cells.

Earlier hunts looked only near gene promoters. This search found EWS-FLI1 binding long repeats of the letters GGAA. Such stretches can act like switches for nearby genes. Those landing spots may be the levers the fusion protein pulls. Pulling them switches genes on and drives the cancer.
plos-pone-0005032:
Musicians rarely slip, but their brains still watch for errors. When can an error be detected? Clemens Maidhof and colleagues recorded brain waves from performing musicians. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They looked for event-related potentials before errors happened. Earlier studies had focused on signals after wrong responses.

Error-related signals appeared before the wrong note sounded. The brain monitors performance in real time, ahead of the fingers. That fast monitoring may allow last-second corrections. It may also explain the feeling of knowing a mistake is coming. The finding shows our inner critic works quickly. It operates even in experts whose movements are highly trained.
plos-pone-0005132:
Some bacteria swap sulfur for oxygen in their DNA backbone. The trait is called phosphorothioation. It was first noticed over twenty years ago in Streptomyces. Hong-Yu Ou and colleagues built a database for it in PLOS ONE in 2009. The database is called dndDB. The name comes from the dnd gene cluster that governs the trait.

Similar clusters are widespread among bacteria. The database collects the genes and chemistry behind them. It maps a weird DNA modification across species. Researchers chasing sulfur-armored genomes gain a reference. Such modifications can protect DNA or mark it as self. They may also matter for biotechnology. A shared database keeps discoveries organized and comparable.
plos-pone-0005232:
Proteins that hold sister chromosomes together are vital for healthy development. Faults in them cause Cornelia de Lange syndrome, with effects across many body systems. Zhang and colleagues varied the dose of one regulator, PDS5, in PLOS ONE in 2009 to see how development responds.

PDS5 helps control chromosome cohesion and has two forms in vertebrates. Changing its amount disturbed mammalian development in their tests. The results show how sensitive embryos are to the dose of cohesion factors, which informs care and research for the group of disorders called cohesinopathies. For parents of children with this syndrome, work of this kind brings the dose needs of the growing body into clear view at last.
plos-pone-0005332:
Several long-term lung diseases share an overactive immune response, with many inflammatory signals and proteases in the lung. Zhang and colleagues proposed a modeling-derived hypothesis for that chronicity in PLOS ONE in 2009, covering diseases such as cystic fibrosis and chronic bronchitis.

In their model, hyperactive IRAK and TRAF6 signaling desensitizes pathogen recognition. A dulled alarm would let germs persist while inflammation keeps raging, a seeming paradox the model resolves. A clear, testable hypothesis like this gives lung researchers a new target list. Lung diseases that drag on for years cost health and wealth, so a model that can be put to the test in mice. In cells is the right next step for this bold claim.
plos-pone-0005932:
Some plant genes must stay silent, or their stray messages can harm the cell. Todd Blevins, Olga Pontes, Craig Pikaard and colleagues studied one such case in the plant Arabidopsis in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper looks at odd transcripts from 5S ribosomal DNA, a set of repeated genes held in dark, packed chromatin.

Two separate guards keep those stray messages down: small RNAs from the repeats, and DDM1, a factor that keeps the DNA packing in place. Each works on its own, the team reports. The study shows how plants layer their defenses to keep a restless gene family quiet, a task every complex genome must solve.
plos-pone-0006032:
Flu shots must be rebuilt each year as the virus drifts, and older adults gain the least from them. Ted Ross, Kutub Mahmood, Corey Crevar and colleagues tested a different build in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper describes a trivalent vaccine made of virus-like particles, empty shells that look like flu but carry no genes, aimed at three seasonal strains.

Mice and ferrets given the shells raised protective immune responses, the title reports. Particles that teach without infecting could be made faster and more safely than grown virus. The platform is also flexible, so it could be tuned as strains change. The work backs a promising route toward stronger flu cover for those at greatest risk.
plos-pone-0006132:
A rare fish's genes can be spread by lending them to a common fish's body. Sullip Majhi, Ricardo Hattori, Masashi Yokota and colleagues advanced that surrogacy in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper transplants germ cells into the gonads of sexually competent adult fish, an approach for rapid propagation of endangered and valuable germlines.

Germ cell transplantation also serves basic study of how germ cells grow and mature. Using adults that can breed at once, rather than waiting for young recipients to mature, speeds every use. For species near extinction, speed is the point: a germline banked in a living surrogate can rebuild a population while habitat work proceeds.
plos-pone-0006232:
Breaking genes at random is a classic way to learn what each gene does. Jorge Vidal and colleagues built a better random mutagenesis tool for Clostridium perfringens in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The toxin-making bacterium causes food poisoning and gas gangrene, but older mutagenesis systems worked poorly in it.

Their EZ-Tn5 based system jumped a marker into random spots of the genome. With it they found a previously unknown locus that controls toxin production. A new control point offers fresh angles on how the bacterium causes disease. The tool itself will serve other studies of this stubborn pathogen.
plos-pone-0006732:
Mahamadou S. Sissoko and colleagues tested a malaria drug combination against a parasitic worm disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. The disease is schistosomiasis caused by Schistosoma haematobium. It infects the urinary tract of many children in Africa. The standard treatment is praziquantel. The test drug paired artesunate with sulfamethoxypyrazine and pyrimethamine, at malaria doses.

School-aged children with the infection received one treatment or the other. The team then compared how well each cleared the parasite. A malaria drug that also cures schistosomiasis would be valuable where both diseases overlap. Mass treatment campaigns could then tackle two diseases together. The trial gives direct evidence on whether that shortcut works.
plos-pone-0006832:
Hossein Khiabanian and his team set the ages of flu cases side by side for two flu types in PLOS ONE in 2009. Two types of influenza A have gone round each year since 1977. They are called H3N2 and H1N1. Each year, both make part of the land sick. The team asked if the two types hit the same age groups.

They did not. The age spread of cases set the two types apart. Gaps like that can mirror who met the germs in past years. They can also guide who gets flu shots first. Side-by-side age data turn plain case counts into clues.
plos-pone-0006932:
Yi-Chieh Nancy Du, David Klimstra, and Harold Varmus used engineered mice to study pancreatic cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. A basic question was unsettled at the time. Do different pancreatic tumors start from different target cells, or from shared precursors? The team switched on an oncogene called PyMT in chosen cell types.

In insulin-producing beta cells, PyMT caused irreversible overgrowth called hyperplasia. In pancreatic progenitor cells, it produced acinar cell carcinomas that depended on the oncogene. The contrast shows that the starting cell shapes the tumor that follows. That insight guides how researchers model and classify pancreatic cancers.
plos-pone-0007032:
Jonathan Bohbot and Joseph Dickens characterized a mosquito smell receptor in PLOS ONE in 2009. Some odor molecules come in mirror-image forms called enantiomers. The forms share the same chemistry but opposite handedness. In insect communication, one form can be active while its mirror is not.

Working with the yellow fever mosquito Aedes aegypti, the pair studied one receptor closely. That receptor could tell mirror-image odors apart. Such selective receptors help mosquitoes find humans and mates by smell. Knowing them may aid new repellents or traps for a major disease carrier.
plos-pone-0007132:
Il-Man Kim and Matthew Wolf built a switchable heart disease model in flies in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dilated cardiomyopathy enlarges the heart chamber and weakens its squeeze. Fruit flies can model the condition, as earlier gene studies showed. The team went further, making the disease inducible and reversible in individual adult flies.

They examined the same fly's heart repeatedly as disease turned on and off. Watching one heart through the whole cycle removes guesswork between animals. A reversible model lets researchers test when damage can still be undone. That timing question is central to heart failure care.
plos-pone-0007232:
Janine Scholefield, L. Jacquie Greenberg, Marc S. Weinberg, and colleagues designed a gene-silencing treatment for a brain disorder in 2009. Spinocerebellar ataxia type 7 is caused by an expanded repeat in DNA. The repeated section makes a faulty protein that drives progressive neurodegeneration, and no treatment existed.

The authors design RNA interference hairpins that silence only the mutant form of ataxin-7. Sparing the normal copy is essential for safety. They report correction of a disease phenotype in their model. Their work tests a precise strategy for other repeat-expansion disorders as well.
plos-pone-0007332:
Bart van de Sluis, Arjan J. Groot, Jeroen Vermeulen, and colleagues studied a regulator of the low-oxygen response in 2009. The protein COMMD1 is linked to copper balance, immune signaling, and sodium transport. The authors had identified COMMD1 as a new player in signaling by HIF-1, the master low-oxygen transcription factor.

Mouse embryos lacking Commd1 showed increased HIF activity. The authors report COMMD1 promotes breakdown of HIF-1 alpha without needing the usual oxygen-dependent pathway. The breakdown involves heat shock proteins HSP90 and HSP70. Their work adds a backup route for controlling oxygen responses in cells.
openalex-w1997401532: Bacteria wear sugar coats — and enzymes decide the patterns. A 2014 study built a network method to find the sugar targets of bacterial glycosyltransferases. The method predicted which sugars the enzymes attach to their targets.
openalex-w2102671432: The Higgs loves bottom quarks — CMS went hunting. The CMS collaboration's 2014 search looked for the Standard Model Higgs produced with a W or Z boson, decaying to bottom quarks. The VH channels tested the Higgs-to-bb coupling.
openalex-w2103574532: Visceral leishmaniasis stalks Brazil — urbanizing and deadly. Gontijo and Melo's 2004 Portuguese review covers visceral leishmaniasis in Brazil: current picture, challenges, and perspectives. The work tracked the disease's spread into cities and its deadly forms.
openalex-w2113108732: What drives HIV among gay men in the US and Peru? Goodreau and colleagues' 2012 study modeled the US and Peruvian HIV epidemics in men who have sex with men. The work estimated transmission shares across partnerships, roles, and infection stages.
openalex-w2114838732: Amazon leaves vary — genes, soil, and climate explain why. A 2009 study analyzed leaf traits across the Amazon Basin. The 1,040-tree, 62-plot analysis weighed family tree, soils, and climate — leaf economics at basin scale, revealed for the first time ever published anywhere.
plos-pone-0006332:
Strep throat bacteria leave immune fingerprints that may misfire in some children with tics. Mauro Bombaci and colleagues screened blood sera from tic patients against a protein array of Group A Streptococcus antigens in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The bacterium also causes severe invasive disease and complications where host antibodies attack the body.

Patients showed a broad and enhanced immune response against the strep antigens. That pattern supports a role for post-strep immunity in tic disorders. Protein arrays let many antigens be tested from tiny blood samples. The study sharpens the hunt for the specific targets involved.
plos-pone-0009732:
Bile ducts carry bile from the liver, and their shape depends on how cells divide. Junnian Zhou and colleagues studied a protein that guides that growth in rat liver cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The protein, epimorphin, regulates duct formation through mitosis orientation. Mitosis orientation is the angle at which a cell splits into two. The work used rat liver epithelial stem-like cells, cells that can help rebuild liver tissue. How cells angle their divisions, the study shows, shapes the growing duct. Liver development depends on such fine control.
openalex-w2472132332: Global climate models see the big picture; regional planners need the local one. This 2016 Geoscientific Model Development paper describes CORDEX — the Coordinated Regional Downscaling Experiment — as a diagnostic project within CMIP6. Building on earlier downscaling comparisons, it provides a common framework for turning coarse global projections into the regional detail decision-makers need.
openalex-w2600399632: Climate models need to know what humanity has emitted — every year since 1750. This 2018 paper presents the Community Emissions Data System (CEDS): annual historical emissions of reactive gases, carbonaceous aerosols, and CO2 from 1750 to 2014. The dataset improves on predecessors and underpins the simulations that project our climate future.
openalex-w2741543132: Einstein's equations for stars usually assume pressure pushes equally in all directions — but real compact objects may not. This 2018 European Physical Journal C paper uses gravitational decoupling via minimal geometric deformation to extend isotropic stellar models to anisotropic ones. The technique offers new solutions for describing ultra-dense stars.
